source_text:
Generative UI
Generative UI is a Dulche capability that allows a model or Agent to return arbitrary structured user interfaces when an interface is more useful than prose. Generated interfaces may be visual, interactive and stateful, but MUST be expressed through a validated declarative Generative UI schema and MUST NOT execute arbitrary model-generated application code.
Rendering and trust boundary
CUI is the rendering layer for Generative UI. Generated surfaces render inside a CUI <GenerativeContainer> or equivalent trusted host component using approved CUI primitives, design tokens, theming, layout, accessibility and interaction behaviour. Any authorised 9to1 app may host a GenerativeContainer without implementing its own incompatible renderer.
Dulche may choose the structure and composition of the interface, including novel layouts, but the model output is data/schema rather than executable JavaScript, Python, shell commands, native binaries or arbitrary application code. The Generative UI runtime validates schema version, component types, properties, state bindings, declared actions and capability references before rendering.
Templates
Generative UI provides reusable high-level templates for common interaction patterns. Templates are starting structures, not hard limits; Dulche can instantiate, extend, combine or restyle them through supported schema properties.
* Flashcard set / study deck.
* Table, sortable/filterable data table and comparison grid.
* Quiz, practice exercise and answer/reveal workflow.
* Timeline and step-by-step guide.
* Checklist and progress tracker.
* Card grid / gallery / result browser.
* Form, questionnaire and multi-step wizard.
* Kanban/task-board style layout where appropriate.
* Glossary / FAQ / concept-reference layout.
* Diagram, relationship map and structured visual explainer.
* Other shared templates added by the Generative UI framework or authorised extensions.
Primitive composition
When no template fully fits the task, Dulche can compose a custom surface from approved lower-level primitives. The supported primitive set should include, where appropriate, text/heading blocks, icons or generated illustrations, cards, badges/tags, buttons, inputs, dropdowns, toggles, sliders, chips, lists, tables, grids, tabs, accordions, progress indicators, layout containers, drag containers, drop zones, connectors/relationships, semantic-object views and other safe CUI primitives.
The primitive library is extensible through versioned framework/extension contracts. Unsupported component types MUST be rejected or downgraded safely; a model cannot create a new privileged executable component merely by naming it in the schema.
State and interaction
Generated surfaces may maintain bounded typed state. Supported interactions can include selecting options, sorting/filtering, expanding/collapsing content, progressing through steps, editing fields, revealing hints/answers, checking responses, reordering items, dragging supported objects between declared drop zones, switching views and updating selected data.
State mutations are handled by the Generative UI runtime or by declared typed actions. Interaction support does not grant the model arbitrary code execution or unrestricted access to the host application's process.
Progressive conversational evolution
A generated surface is a first-class conversation artifact and may evolve across turns. Dulche should be able to patch or transform an existing surface instead of rebuilding unrelated output from scratch. Examples include turning a static explanation into an interactive exercise, adding another column to a table, converting notes into flashcards, adding filters, changing a card grid into a comparison view or preserving quiz progress while adding new questions.
Updates must address stable SurfaceID/component/state identities or equivalent schema identities so user interaction state is retained wherever the requested transformation allows it. Partial regeneration is preferred when only part of a surface changes.
Typed actions and side effects
Generated controls bind to declared typed actions rather than arbitrary executable handlers. An action definition includes stable identity, expected input schema, allowed state mutation or API binding, required capability/permission and result/error contract.
Pure presentation and local interaction may execute inside the Generative UI runtime without external side effects. Actions that invoke 9to1 APIs, tools or external services remain subject to the same permission, confirmation, auditing and consequence rules as the underlying capability. Generative UI MUST NOT be a path around security prompts or tool permissions.
Data binding and semantic objects
Generative UI can bind to authorised structured data and canonical 9to1 entities instead of flattening everything into prompt text. Examples include Data ranges, Planner tasks, Maps Places/Routes, Board items, Write selections/documents, search results, translation sets, code diffs or Dulche Action Graph state.
Bindings retain source identity and permissions. A rendered card or table row that represents a canonical object should reference that object rather than silently creating a disconnected copy unless the user explicitly asks for a snapshot.
Ephemeral and saved artifacts
A generated surface may remain ephemeral to the current response/session or be promoted through an explicit supported conversion/save path. Examples include saving generated flashcards as a study resource, converting a generated task board into a Board, inserting a generated table into Write/Data or saving a generated route through Maps. Promotion uses the destination app's canonical API and permissions.
Third-party visual examples and assets
Generative UI may reproduce the functional idea or spatial structure needed to explain a third-party product/game without copying proprietary artwork merely to imitate the source. Where licensed/authorised assets are not available, it should use generic, stylised, text-labelled or newly generated representations sufficient to communicate the concept.
Example: if the user asks how an item is crafted in Minecraft, Dulche may create a visual 3x3 crafting-grid representation using generic/stylised ingredient tokens and an output slot rather than copied official item textures or proprietary interface artwork. In later turns the same surface may be made interactive using approved drag/drop primitives so the user can move ingredient tokens, receive validation, request hints or turn the recipe into a quiz.
Accessibility and visual consistency
Generated UI MUST inherit the host CUI theme/design system and remain accessible. The runtime should enforce semantic roles, labels, focusability/order, keyboard operation, screen-reader information, non-colour-only meaning and accessible alternatives for interactions such as drag/drop wherever the component library supports them.
Failure and fallback
Invalid, unsupported or unsafe generated schemas MUST fail closed without executing arbitrary content. Dulche may repair/regenerate the affected surface or fall back to a non-interactive/native representation while preserving the user-visible answer where possible.
Result contract and acceptance
Result.GeneratedUI contains the generated UI payload when present and returns null when no generated interface is produced. The payload must identify schema version, surface identity, component tree, declared state/bindings and declared actions/capabilities required to reproduce the surface safely.
* Dulche can create arbitrary useful UI structures without arbitrary code execution.
* Built-in templates and lower-level CUI primitives can be combined and extended within the declarative schema.
* Generated surfaces support safe stateful interaction and can evolve across conversation turns without unnecessarily discarding user state.
* All external side effects route through typed permission-aware actions.
* Structured 9to1 data can be bound by canonical identity, and generated artifacts can be promoted through destination-app APIs.
* Generated UI follows CUI theming/accessibility and safely handles invalid schemas or unavailable components.
Background Learning
Background Learning is an explicitly opt-in Dulche personalisation subsystem. It is separate from Persistent Memory. Enabling Background Learning allows Dulche to learn useful patterns, interests and reusable knowledge from eligible 9to1 activity over time; it does not itself enable or disable Persistent Memory and it does not imply continuous fine-tuning of the underlying base model.
Eligible learning classes
Background Learning can maintain three broad classes of learned information:
* 9to1 usage and project context: which authorised surfaces the user uses most, recurring workflows, recently or frequently active projects, apps commonly used together, important project terminology/entities and other usage patterns that improve contextual relevance.
* Interests and topic Knowledge Banks: recurring subjects the user appears to care about, together with reusable factual/reference material that can improve later answers and remain available offline. For example, repeated questions about cars may lead to an Interest record for cars and a local Cars Knowledge Bank containing useful terminology, concepts and sourced reference material.
* Other relevant personalisation information: additional permitted information that materially improves responses, such as preferred terminology, recurring goals, explanation preferences, established project conventions, frequently used tools, entity relationships and corrections that should influence future response behaviour.
Usage and project learning
The usage-learning layer SHOULD retain useful semantic state rather than an indiscriminate permanent clickstream. For example, it may learn that Dev and Stack are frequently used for a particular project or that a project is currently active. Raw activity used to derive these signals should be retained only to the extent required by the configured retention/privacy model.
Learned project context can help Dulche resolve ambiguous references, rank context candidates, suggest likely relevant surfaces and prepare authorised Agents with useful project context. It MUST remain scope-aware: project-specific learning does not automatically become unrelated global context.
Interest Knowledge Banks
Background Learning can create and maintain topic-specific KnowledgeBank entities. A KnowledgeBank can contain a stable ID, topic/title, entries, source/provenance metadata, confidence, freshness, creation/update state, storage/sync policy and enabled/disabled state. Knowledge Banks may be created automatically from recurring interests or explicitly managed by the user.
Knowledge Bank entries may include reusable summaries, terminology, relationships, reference facts and other material previously obtained from authorised local sources, user interactions or trusted retrieval. Factual entries MUST retain enough provenance/freshness information for Dulche to distinguish durable knowledge from information that may need refreshing.
Knowledge Banks are not the same as Persistent Memory. For example, 'the user is interested in cars' is personalisation/user context; a structured offline bank explaining engines, EV charging and vehicle terminology is subject knowledge. Dulche may use both when relevant, but they remain separately inspectable and manageable.
Structured learned state
Background Learning MUST store structured learned records rather than relying on one opaque free-form profile. Records should carry stable identity, category/type, subject/entity, learned value, provenance, confidence, creation/update state, last reinforcement/use where useful, freshness/expiry semantics and user-edited/locked state where applicable.
Explicit user corrections outrank contradictory inferred learning. If a user corrects an inferred preference, project status or interest, the system MUST revise/supersede the stale inference instead of allowing both to compete indefinitely as equally valid facts.
Selective retrieval
The complete learning store MUST NOT be injected into every request. Dulche must retrieve only learning context relevant to the active request, Agent, app and permission scope. Retrieval should use current entities/topics/project context to select the smallest useful set of records and Knowledge Bank material.
Privacy and cloud boundaries
Background Learning data is private by default and exists to personalise the user's 9to1 AI experience. It MUST NOT be sold, used to build advertising profiles or indiscriminately uploaded to third parties. Enabling Background Learning does not itself grant permission to transmit learned information to a cloud model/provider.
If a Dulche request uses a remote/cloud provider, disclosure of any learned context remains subject to the normal provider, privacy, permission and data-minimisation rules for that request. The implementation MUST distinguish permission to learn/store information from permission to disclose that information externally.
Any optional cross-device synchronisation of Background Learning state must be user-controlled and protected by the applicable authenticated/encrypted 9to1 sync/storage architecture. The feature MUST remain useful locally and must not require insecure cloud upload merely to personalise responses.
User controls
Users must be able to enable/disable Background Learning, pause new learning, inspect learned information, inspect and manage topic Knowledge Banks, correct inaccurate learning, delete individual learned records or a complete topic bank, clear learned categories and configure which apps/projects/categories may contribute where supported. Disabling learning stops creation/reinforcement of new learned state but MUST NOT silently delete existing Persistent Memory or unrelated user data.
Relationship to Persistent Memory
Persistent Memory and Background Learning are independent. Persistent Memory stores durable cross-session memories under the Memory policy; Background Learning is the opt-in process that derives usage patterns, interests, Knowledge Banks and other personalisation state. Neither feature may silently enable, disable, clear or substitute for the other.
Background Learning may identify information that would be useful as a durable memory, but any conversion into Persistent Memory must use the Memory subsystem and preserve that the source was an inference rather than an explicit user statement. Explicit Memory corrections remain authoritative over contradictory Background Learning inferences.
Background Learning acceptance requirements
* Background Learning is off until the user opts in and remains independently configurable from Persistent Memory.
* Eligible 9to1 usage/project patterns, interests/Knowledge Banks and other useful personalisation information can be learned as structured, inspectable state.
* Topic Knowledge Banks can provide relevant offline reference material and retain provenance/freshness sufficient to avoid presenting stale inferred facts as timeless truth.
* Only relevant learning context is retrieved for a request; the full learning store is not injected indiscriminately.
* Learned data is not sold, used for advertising profiles or uploaded to cloud providers merely because learning is enabled.
* Users can inspect, correct, scope and delete learning independently of Persistent Memory.
MCP Support
MCP is a first-class Dulche extension/runtime capability. Dulche MUST support acting as an MCP client for authorised local/remote MCP servers and acting as an MCP server when 9-1 intentionally exposes approved capabilities to external MCP clients. MCP execution MUST use the same permission, audit, cancellation, timeout and structured-error contracts as native Dulche tools.

Built-in Persistent skill
Dulche MUST ship a first-party built-in Skill with the canonical display name Persistent and a stable reserved SkillID. Activating Persistent on a request sets that root request's PersistencePolicy to Persistent. The Skill is declarative: it changes Runtime orchestration semantics and does not gain permissions, tools, external access, budget or trust merely by being active.
Persistent activation MUST be explicit and visible in request metadata, the compose invocation state, FullLog and Action Graph. It MAY be invoked through the shared @ resource picker as @Persistent. The active version MUST be recorded like every other Skill so later inspection can prove which persistence contract governed the run.
The Persistent Skill MUST use the canonical Dulche persistent-request contract. In particular, an ordinary checkpoint, context compaction boundary, provider lease expiry, model restart, recoverable tool timeout or similar continuation boundary MUST NOT be treated as successful completion of the turn. The Runtime preserves/reconstructs execution state and continues under the same RootRequestID until the task's completion criteria are actually satisfied, the user explicitly stops it, or all remaining work is non-terminally AwaitingUser because of an unresolved blocker.
While a Persistent turn is running, an ordinary follow-up message sent by the user MUST join the same root turn as a SteeringMessage and MUST NOT implicitly cancel, replace or interrupt the active work. Dulche consumes the message at the next safe planning boundary, updates the plan and continues. Explicit Stop, explicit replace/edit semantics and any separately exposed interrupt/stack action retain their distinct meanings.
A blocker that cannot be resolved within the request's effective permission and capability bounds MUST be surfaced to the user as a structured blocker immediately. The blocker MUST isolate only the dependent work. Dulche MUST continue any independent runnable work in the same persistent turn; if no independent work remains, the turn enters AwaitingUser without being misreported as complete or timed out. When the blocker is resolved, the same durable turn resumes from current state rather than silently restarting completed work.
Persistent MUST remain compatible with automatic context compaction, Context Summarisation, Subagents, checkpoints, crash recovery and provider/model fallback. None of those mechanisms may erase completed side-effect evidence, duplicate consequential actions or weaken permission/approval requirements.

source_text:
External App Integrations
External App Integrations is the shared 9to1 framework for connecting, authenticating and operating third-party accounts/services. Authentication, provider scopes, transport, sync, webhooks, rate limits, provider-specific errors and remote-entity identity MUST be encapsulated by this shared layer rather than reimplemented independently inside each consuming app.
Core connection model
The framework MUST define stable typed entities for IntegrationProvider, Connection, ExternalAccount, IntegrationCapability, CredentialReference, RemoteEntityReference, SyncCursor, WebhookSubscription and ConnectionHealth or equivalent contracts. A Connection represents one authenticated provider/account relationship and has stable identity independent of whichever 9to1 app first created it.
Multiple accounts/connections for the same provider MUST be supported. For example, a user may connect separate personal and work Google accounts or multiple GitHub identities without those accounts being merged or ambiguously selected.
Connect once, reuse through authorised capabilities
A provider account should be connected once through the integration framework and then reused by authorised 9to1 surfaces. Consuming apps MUST request capabilities from the existing Connection rather than maintaining private duplicate credentials or running their own hidden authentication flows.
Examples include a Google connection supplying Drive capabilities to Files, Gmail capabilities to Mail, Calendar capabilities to Planner/Calendar and Contacts capabilities to relevant people pickers; a GitHub connection may supply repository/issue/pull-request capabilities to Stack, Dev or authorised Dulche Agents. The exact provider capabilities available remain determined by granted provider scopes and the integration adapter.
Provider scope versus 9to1 permission
Provider authorisation and 9to1 authorisation are separate gates. A Connection may possess provider scopes that a particular app, Agent, Skill, Plugin or extension is not authorised to use. Both the remote provider scope and the applicable 9to1 permission/capability policy MUST allow an operation before it is executed.
Connecting an account MUST NOT implicitly grant every 9to1 surface unrestricted access to that account. Permission decisions should be made at an appropriate capability/resource scope and remain inspectable/revocable.
Typed capability contracts
Consuming apps SHOULD depend on provider-neutral typed capabilities where equivalent semantics exist instead of embedding provider-specific endpoint logic. Examples include Files.List/Read/Upload, Mail.Search/Read/Send, Calendar.ListEvents/CreateEvent, Contacts.Search, Git.ListRepositories/CreateIssue and Chat.ListMessages or equivalent canonical contracts.
Provider adapters map those typed capabilities onto the provider's API. Provider-specific features that cannot be represented faithfully through a common contract may be exposed through explicit provider-namespaced capabilities; the common abstraction MUST NOT silently discard important provider semantics merely to force false parity.
Capability schemas MUST declare input/output shape, supported operations, required provider scopes, relevant 9to1 permissions, pagination/streaming behaviour, provider limitations and error states.
Authentication and credential storage
The integration framework centrally owns supported authentication flows such as OAuth/OIDC, PKCE, device-code flows, API-key authentication or provider-specific enterprise methods where appropriate. Apps MUST NOT request or persist reusable provider credentials directly when the integration framework can broker them.
Credential material such as access tokens, refresh tokens, API keys, passwords and private keys MUST live in approved secure credential storage. Integration records, Den records, logs, exports and app settings store credential references/connection identities rather than plaintext reusable secrets.
Token refresh, expiry, revocation and provider reauthentication are lifecycle concerns of the integration framework. A consumer receives a capability result or typed authentication-required failure, not raw credentials it can reuse arbitrarily.
Scope escalation
If a Connection exists but lacks a provider scope required by a new capability, the consuming surface requests scope escalation through the shared integration framework. The user must be shown which additional provider access is being requested and why. The framework extends/replaces the existing authorisation where the provider supports it rather than creating a hidden duplicate connection.
Remote identity and canonical 9to1 entities
External objects MUST retain their remote identity and provenance. A RemoteEntityReference should identify the provider, Connection, remote object ID, remote revision/version where available, remote URL/reference and any mapped canonical 9to1 entity.
Opening or referencing a remote object does not automatically create a separate canonical copy. The UI and APIs MUST distinguish operations such as Open remote, Import/copy into 9to1, Link/reference and Keep synchronised.
Where an external object is mapped to a canonical 9to1 entity, the relationship must remain explicit so the system does not create multiple disconnected local copies of the same remote item or accidentally treat provider IDs as globally unique without Connection/provider context.
Live, cached, imported and synchronised state
The integration layer MUST distinguish live remote data, cached metadata, cached content, imported local copies and synchronised mirrors. Consuming apps must be able to determine whether displayed information is current, cached, stale or locally diverged.
Caching policies must respect provider terms, account permissions, data sensitivity and user settings. A cached object must not be presented as live merely because a prior request succeeded.
Sync, webhooks and change feeds
Where a provider supports webhooks, push notifications or incremental change feeds, the integration framework SHOULD use them rather than each app independently polling the same account. It owns webhook registration/renewal/validation, change cursors, deduplication, retry/backoff and background refresh.
Polling remains available where required by the provider or capability, but should be centralised enough to avoid redundant traffic and quota consumption. Sync state must include sufficient cursor/revision information to continue incrementally after restart or temporary offline periods.
Offline and queued-operation behaviour
Consumers may continue to display authorised cached state while a provider is unavailable, but the stale/offline state and last successful sync/freshness information MUST remain visible when material. The framework MUST NOT silently claim remote mutations succeeded when they have only been queued locally.
If queued remote writes are supported, each operation needs stable identity, retry/idempotency semantics, dependency ordering where applicable, visible pending/failed state and explicit conflict handling. Reconnection must not blindly replay an action that is no longer valid or that already completed remotely.
Conflicts and versioning
For synchronised/mirrored objects, use provider revision identifiers, ETags/version tokens or equivalent change metadata where available. Wall-clock timestamps alone MUST NOT be the only conflict authority.
Compatible disjoint edits may be merged where the owning capability can prove a safe merge. Otherwise preserve both versions or surface a conflict to the owning app/user. Provider-side deletion, permission loss and remote moves/renames require explicit typed states rather than being treated as generic missing-file errors.
Connection health and failure states
Connections expose typed health/lifecycle states such as Connected, AuthenticationRequired, ScopeRequired, RateLimited, ProviderUnavailable, Degraded, SyncError, Revoked and Disabled or equivalent. Apps consume these states and present appropriate user-facing recovery rather than leaking raw HTTP/provider exceptions.
Health information should include the failing capability/provider account where relevant, last successful contact/sync, retryability and the action required from the user when one exists.
Rate limits and reliability
The shared layer MUST centrally support pagination, retry-after handling, provider quotas, transient network retries, exponential backoff/jitter, idempotency, request cancellation, partial response handling and provider-specific service limits. Consuming apps MUST NOT each invent incompatible retry/quota behaviour.
Connection management UI
9to1 MUST provide a central integrations management surface, hosted under the appropriate Home/Settings area, showing provider, connected account identity, connection status, provider-granted scopes/capabilities, authorised 9to1 consumers where exposed, recent/last successful activity, errors, reconnect/re-authorise, permission management and disconnect/revoke actions.
Individual apps may deep-link into this management flow or expose capability-specific connection prompts, but connection state remains owned by the shared framework.
Dulche and Agent access
Dulche, Agents and AI surfaces use External App Integrations through the same typed capabilities and permissions as first-party apps. Dulche does not own a parallel account-authentication layer.
For example, a request to find an email uses an authorised Mail capability for an existing connection; a request to create a GitHub issue uses the relevant Git capability. Normal Dulche tool/action permissions and consequential-action confirmation requirements still apply. Merely connecting an account does not grant every Agent permission to mutate it.
Relationship to Plugins and MCP
External App Integrations, Plugins and MCP are distinct abstractions. External App Integrations represent durable authenticated third-party account/service relationships and their capabilities. Plugins are installable packages that may add executable/integrated functionality. MCP is a protocol by which Dulche can discover/use tools/resources.
They may interoperate: a Plugin may register a provider adapter; an integration capability may be surfaced to Dulche through an approved tool/MCP bridge. Such composition MUST preserve the underlying Connection identity, provider scopes and 9to1 permission checks rather than laundering authority through another abstraction.
Provider SDK and extension
9to1 SHOULD expose a versioned Integration Provider SDK/manifest contract so additional providers can be implemented without changing every consuming app. A provider definition can declare provider identity/branding metadata, authentication method, capability schemas, provider scopes, remote entity types, webhook/change-feed support, rate-limit semantics, health checks and provider-specific settings.
Third-party provider adapters remain sandboxed/permissioned according to their implementation model. Registering a provider does not grant unrestricted access to other Connections, credential stores or unrelated local data.
Disconnect and revocation
Disconnect semantics MUST be explicit and predictable. Disconnecting a Connection should stop sync/background activity, invalidate or remove local credential references as appropriate, disable provider capabilities and clear/expire caches according to policy. Where supported and requested, provider-side token revocation should also be attempted.
Disconnecting an account MUST NOT automatically delete unrelated local 9to1 artifacts previously imported from it. For linked/synchronised objects, the UI must explain what local data remains, what becomes unavailable and whether any pending remote operations are abandoned.
Security invariants
* Possessing a provider credential does not grant any app, Agent, Skill, Plugin or extension unrestricted access to the associated account.
* Every external operation must pass both provider scope/capability validation and the relevant 9to1 permission boundary.
* Consuming apps receive capability access/results, not raw reusable credentials.
* Connection/account identity, remote-object identity, provenance and provider limitations must remain explicit across app boundaries.
* Logs, exports and Den records must not contain plaintext reusable provider secrets.
External App Integrations acceptance requirements
* One authenticated Connection can be reused safely by multiple authorised 9to1 apps without duplicated credentials or hidden per-app OAuth implementations.
* Multiple accounts per provider are unambiguous and stable.
* Typed provider-neutral capabilities work where semantics align, with provider-specific extensions exposed explicitly rather than silently discarded.
* Provider scopes and 9to1 consumer permissions are enforced as independent gates.
* Live/cached/imported/synchronised states, remote identity and conflict/version state remain explicit and recoverable.
* Webhooks/change feeds, polling, retries, rate limits, queued operations and connection health are handled centrally with deterministic failure semantics.
* Dulche/Agents use the same connection/capability layer and cannot bypass account permissions.
* Disconnect/revocation, secure credential storage and provider SDK integration are implemented without deleting unrelated local artifacts or exposing reusable secrets.

LE-02 — Package contract and lifecycle
The native package manifest MUST classify each stable PackageID/version as mandatory shared core, optional app, app-required dependency or optional feature dependency. The mandatory-shared rule takes precedence when a component is both shared and niche. Mandatory means installed, not eagerly started or loaded into memory. Record dependency version ranges, platform/architecture support, integrity/signature metadata, activation requirements and reverse dependencies using Home's existing package service.
The single trusted installer MUST install Home, all mandatory modules, the selected app and its app-required dependencies. Selecting a second app MUST reuse compatible shared packages. Internal platform package formats may be used; separate user-facing standalone MSIX installers for individual apps are not the distribution model. Native Windows and 9to1-OS use this contract through their supported packaging mechanisms. Browser apps use authenticated shared web services and MUST NOT require a local Home installation.

LE-07 — Chat storage, transfer and privacy contract
Storage mode is a property of the existing canonical conversation and its managed attachments/derived records, not a separate Local Chats database. Local permits storage on the current device only; Mesh permits authorised replicas across devices in the selected personal/team namespace; Cloud adds encrypted account-storage backup to that Mesh scope. All Mesh Devices never means every device in an unrelated organisation. A newly created chat defaults to Local unless the user has explicitly chosen another eligible default. Existing chats retain their known placement on upgrade; do not migrate them silently.
Persist ConversationID, requested/effective storage mode, authorised namespace/destination DeviceIDs, storage-policy revision and transfer state through the existing Spaces/Den/Files/Home contracts. Transfers expose JobID and per-destination Pending, Transferring, Synced, Failed or Blocked state with revision acknowledgements and retry/cancel controls. Cloud access requires a server-authoritative paid entitlement and StorageAllocatedBytes greater than 10,000,000,000 bytes; available quota is a separate check. Exactly 10 GB does not qualify, and a client label or Send to Cloud action cannot bypass entitlement checks.
Send to Cloud is an explicit promotion. Send to Device previews one authorised Mesh destination and sends only there; it does not silently enable full Mesh or Cloud mode. The destination initially retains that received chat locally. Transfers preserve canonical history/branches and do not replay stored requests or tools. Independent edits reconcile through existing revision/branch conflict rules, never silent last-write-wins.
Before widening placement, show the destination/account, affected conversation and attachment scope, encryption/permission state and quota impact. Commit the widened policy only through authorised domain actions; pending transfers are not reported as complete. Cancellation or interruption retains a valid source copy and exposes any already completed destination copies. Retries are idempotent and recheck permissions, device revocation and entitlements.
Reducing placement stops new replication immediately. The UI MUST distinguish future sync policy from deletion of existing replicas. Show existing copies and offer an explicit, recoverable removal/reassignment flow under the owning storage policy. Offline cleanup remains pending until acknowledged; do not claim remote copies or external backups have been erased without evidence. Billing expiry/quota failure preserves local work and blocks newly unauthorised cloud writes rather than destroying the sole copy.
Temporary chats are always local-only. Their messages, attachments and derived chat state MUST NOT enter Mesh, account backup or durable cross-Space memory while temporary. Save creates a durable local conversation first; a separate authorised action is needed to widen placement. Direct UI/API/Automation transfer attempts on an unsaved temporary chat return TemporaryChatMustBeSaved.
Storage locality and AI/tool execution locality are separate controls. A Local chat MUST NOT be uploaded for account storage or silently exposed through sync, search indexes, telemetry, memory or logging. Remote model/tool processing is allowed only through the separately authorised privacy route, clearly disclosed; a configured cloud fallback alone is not permission. Enforce the global Privacy Ceiling, encryption and log-minimisation rules. User copy must describe verified behaviour, not promise absolute privacy or treat restrained wording as permission for accidental uploads.
Acceptance: inspect network/storage effects for Local and temporary chats; reject temporary transfers through UI and API; save then explicitly promote; send to one device without propagating to others; enforce paid, exact-threshold, quota and revoked-device failures; interrupt/retry transfers without duplicate history; handle offline conflicts; verify downshift/replica-cleanup status and denial of unauthorised cloud-model fallback.

LE-09 — Revision Bank ownership and operations
Revision Bank is a persistent Study resource catalogue over canonical artifacts, not a second file store. It includes created revision materials, existing materials explicitly enrolled/imported and future materials classified by an authorised rule; it MUST NOT silently expose unrelated private documents. Each ResourceID records owning app, canonical ArtifactID/FileID or source reference, resource type, subject/topic links, category membership, provenance, owner/scope and revision. Files/owning apps retain payload, sharing, history and deletion authority.
Recommended, All, Flashcards, Notes, Papers and Quizzes are the default category tabs. Custom categories such as Homework have stable IDs and configurable order. Automatic creation of a category for an uncovered material type is opt-in and idempotent. Categories are filters/membership views, not duplicated artifacts. Recommended draws from recorded difficult/neglected topics and authorised linked resources, with an honest empty state when no match exists.
+ Create New MUST remain right-aligned on the category row and expose Describe a Resource, Flashcard, Quiz, Document, Presentation, Canvas, Board and Other (Dev). Creation routes through Cards, Forms, Write, Present, Canvas, Boards and Dev respectively. Describe a Resource uses Dulche to select an appropriate existing owning type and perform authorised creation; it does not invent another resource app. A failed or cancelled creation must not leave a false completed Bank entry.
Resources open in the real owning-app viewer/interactor embedded in Spaces, with an explicit switch to permitted editing. Open in App is available from both resource and tab context menus and an accessible non-right-click route. Both views address the same artifact. Missing apps/modules follow LE-02; revoked sources cannot remain readable through cached previews or recommendations.
Users can add/enrol, search/filter, classify, reclassify, remove from Bank, open, create and recover supported resources through typed APIs. Remove from Bank removes catalogue membership only; deleting the source is a distinct confirmed owning-app operation. Source rename/move/delete/restore and permission changes update the catalogue incrementally while preserving identity. Persisting an inline-generated flashcard set or quiz uses Cards or Forms canonical data, not a screenshot-only copy.
Acceptance: create each named resource type through the menu; restart; find it in the correct category; edit it embedded and reopen the same ID in its app; rename/move its file; remove only its Bank membership; restore a source; revoke sharing; verify opt-in category creation and source-backed recommendations without duplicated content.

LE-10 — Cards canonical product contract
Cards is a first-party CUI app. No external app donor is selected by this section. It MUST ship through the normal app catalogue, modular installer, Files/open-with and registered preview/editor paths, with the global launch screen, settings, permissions and contextual AI bar. Windows, 9to1-OS and web retain the same canonical flashcard model; other already-supported client obligations remain active. A platform constraint must be declared and tested, not hidden behind an empty app shell or assumed mobile fallback.
A CardSet has stable SetID/ArtifactID, title, owner/scope, ordered CardID membership, subject/topic references, assets and schema/revision metadata. Each Card has stable CardID, editable Front and Back structured content, metadata and revision. Sets and topics organise the same cards; changing a view/grouping does not duplicate content. Shared deck content and a user's ReviewRecord are distinct: review state records principal, CardID, optional TopicID, red/amber/green rating, evidence type and reviewed-at time without publishing another learner's private progress.
Front/back content MUST preserve the specified formatting, font choice, background colour, images, graphs and freehand ink as editable structured data through the Shared Productivity Engine and owning object contracts. Markdown-like formatting is a visual authoring capability, not permission to flatten graphs/ink into text. Native save/export is versioned and round-trips all supported data. Import/export reports unsupported constructs and preserves the source; it does not silently discard unknown required fields.
Required operations are create/open/save, edit either side, add/duplicate/reorder/remove/restore cards, bulk create/edit, search/filter, set/topic/custom grouping, asset insertion, drawing, rate/review, import/export and settings. Bulk edits expose exact per-item results where partial success is allowed; destructive bulk changes have impact preview and the inherited approval rules. Undo/redo and interrupted-save recovery preserve the prior valid revision.
The focused-card view retains partially visible, shadowed neighbours. Vertical scrolling is the default; horizontal navigation is a persisted option. Provide keyboard/touch navigation, the floating search bar and the subject/topic sidebar without obstructing content. Edit mode uses click-to-edit and an explicit Flip button. View mode uses click-to-flip and cannot mutate card content; rating is permitted as personal review state. The AI bar's Write setting does not override the host's View restriction.
A rating MUST persist on the card's personal review record. When a valid Study topic link exists, it MUST submit attributed evidence to the existing Study service and update linked views. An unlinked card remains usable and offers topic linking rather than fabricating a mapping. Shared deck edits do not overwrite other users' review records. Inline Spaces flashcards and Revision Bank entries must be able to open/save the same canonical set.
Acceptance: create a multi-card set with distinct front/back text, rich formatting, image, graph and ink; bulk edit and undo; switch navigation/grouping; search; save/restart and native export/import without loss; prove View cannot edit; rate linked and unlinked cards; verify Study linkage, private per-user reviews, shared-edit conflicts, crash recovery and the same set in Cards, Spaces and Revision Bank. Large sets MUST virtualise card views and bound image/graph/ink caches.

LE-11 — Planner Burrows contract
A Burrow is a named planning context over existing Planner entities, not a duplicate calendar engine or a copy of events/tasks/assignments. It has stable BurrowID, name/icon, owner/scope, ordering, archive state and revision. Native items may have one BurrowID or be Unassigned; the All view includes authorised items across burrows without duplicate identities. Existing items remain Unassigned unless the user assigns them or an existing explicit association provides a deterministic migration.
Study has one canonical Study burrow per owning Study scope, created idempotently and referenced by ID rather than the display name. A custom Minecraft burrow is an independent user-created context. Study's Planner button opens its Study burrow inside the real Planner surface, and Open in App preserves the burrow selection and canonical item identities.
Users MUST be able to create, rename, reorder, select, set a default, archive/recover and delete a burrow; assign/reassign/unassign existing events, PlannerTasks, assignments and other supported planning items; and filter normal Planner views by burrow or All/Unassigned. New items created within a selected burrow inherit that assignment. Moving between burrows changes organisation only, not event time, recurrence, provider calendar, attendees or reminder identity.
Provider-backed items retain provider IDs and permissions. Burrow membership may be local 9to1 metadata and MUST NOT silently move or duplicate the external item. Recurring-item assignment requires an explicit occurrence/series scope using Planner's existing recurrence rules. A burrow's visibility never grants access to otherwise private contained items.
Deleting a burrow MUST preview its item count and reassign its items to a chosen authorised burrow or Unassigned; it must not delete the events/tasks/assignments. Archive hides the context without destroying membership. Reminders continue under existing item policies, regardless of whether a burrow is currently visible.
Acceptance: keep Study and Minecraft items distinct while All shows both once; create and move items without changed IDs/times/reminders; restart; edit a recurring series with explicit scope; handle a read-only external event's local grouping; delete/recover a burrow without losing planning items; verify embedded and standalone Planner use the same state.
LE-12 — API, state and failure contracts
Every new UI action MUST use the same typed domain operation as automation. Extend existing namespaces rather than introducing parallel services: Home package install/update/repair; Spaces Sidebar sections/items/rules, Tabs, conversation placement/transfers, Study recommendations and RevisionBank; 9to1.Cards sets/cards/content/reviews; and 9to1.Planner.Burrows with Create, Get, List, Update, Assign, Unassign, Archive, Restore and Delete.
Before consumers implement against them, owners MUST publish the versioned action catalogue with exact argument/result schemas, affected stable IDs, owner/scope, required permissions, risk/reversibility, expectedRevision for writes, pagination for lists and operationId for replayable mutations. Long operations return JobID/status/cancellation and per-target outcomes. Read/search/preview/context and write APIs enforce the same current permissions; client-supplied account, Space or Burrow IDs do not grant access.
At minimum expose the UI-equivalent create/read/update/organise/delete/recover/import/export/configuration actions, Cards Rate and review queries, RevisionBank Add/Remove/Classify/Recommend/Create/Open, Sidebar AddSection/AddItem/Move/SetRule/Reset, Tabs Open/Select/Move/Close/Restore, and conversation GetPlacement/SetPlacement/SendToCloud/SendToDevice/GetTransfer/CancelTransfer. Public naming must remain within the existing canonical namespace conventions. Internal representations may vary only if these observable semantics remain compatible.
Use the existing structured error envelope. Add specific codes where absent for DependencyRequired, PackageDependencyConflict, TabTargetUnavailable, SidebarRuleInvalid, ProtectedSidebarItem, StorageModeDenied, TemporaryChatMustBeSaved, EntitlementRequired, QuotaExceeded, DeviceRevoked, TransferInterrupted, RevisionConflict, ResourceUnavailable, UnsupportedCardContent and BurrowNotFound. Errors identify action/target, retryability, retained source state and any completed/failed/skipped targets. Unknown/unavailable values are not fabricated defaults.
Persistent schemas MUST be versioned, revision-aware and crash-safe. Permission checks occur again on reconnect/commit. Repeated requests do not duplicate sets, memberships, planning items or transfers. Independent edits can merge only under the owning contract; conflicting edits preserve recoverable versions or return an explicit conflict. Normal deletion is recoverable; permanent purge remains a separate elevated operation. Migrations inspect and preserve actual existing data rather than assuming there is none.
LE-13 — Worker ownership and integration order
The coordinator first maps inherited requirements and affected source areas, then agrees shared manifests/APIs and test fixtures. Assign bounded owners for package/runtime modularity; Spaces navigation/sidebar/tabs/usage; conversation placement/privacy; Study/Revision Bank/Cards; and Planner Burrows. Workers may proceed in parallel only with non-overlapping owned files or explicit coordination. Consumers use reviewed interfaces, not independently invented schemas or duplicate shared components.
Integrate completed units continuously into the accepted root with owning tests and exact-head regression checks. Validate a shared component before dependent surfaces claim completion. Treat existing user feedback and P0/P1 defects as priority work. Packaging changes must re-test app embeds and missing-app paths; chat placement changes must re-test memory, indexing, Voice/Spaces conversation continuity and Mesh; Cards/Study changes must re-test the shared progress service.
The implementation must deliver real connected behaviour, not documentation or UI stubs. An external approval or unavailable device isolates its affected verification/deployment gate; other runnable work continues. The coordinator reviews worker output and remains responsible for final integration and evidence.
LE-14 — Pass acceptance and release exit gate
The acceptance ledger MUST cover every LE group and its inherited requirements with actual UI and API journeys, persistence/restart, permission denial/revocation, interruption/retry/recovery and platform/package evidence. Run populated desktop, narrow/touch, keyboard-only, screen-reader, 200% scaling, theme/contrast and reduced-motion checks. Inspect rendered interfaces, including selected/loading/empty/error/overflow states, not just source code.
Required end-to-end journey: install Spaces with mandatory core; add a custom Study sidebar section using + Add and rearrange it; create a Cards set from Revision Bank, edit both sides and save; reopen the same set in Cards and Spaces; record a topic-linked review and observe Study progress/recommendations; create a Study-burrow assignment and see the same item in standalone Planner; restart and verify all canonical IDs and saved state remain intact. Exercise a missing optional app during this journey and complete its trusted installation without losing context.
Privacy journey: create a temporary local chat, verify no managed off-device copy, reject an unsaved transfer, save locally, send to one authorised device, then explicitly enable eligible Cloud mode. Interrupt/retry a transfer, revoke a destination, and reduce placement while reporting outstanding replica cleanup truthfully. Verify a denied remote AI route cannot be enabled merely by model fallback or by embedding the chat elsewhere.
Resource and reliability evidence MUST state actual hardware/platform, dataset size, active/inactive tab counts, timing and memory/storage observations. Exercise long chat lists, many tabs, large card sets and mixed revision materials. Use approved project budgets where defined; where a release budget is absent, record measured results and the proposed release baseline for approval rather than inventing a passing number. No unbounded cache, polling loop or full-history rescan may substitute for bounded incremental behaviour.
Deliver release artifacts and a manifest identifying product/platform, version, exact commit, cryptographic hash, launch/install instructions and known limitations. Re-run clean install, upgrade, dependency failure, repair and rollback against those exact artifacts. Implementation, verification, deployment and public release approval remain distinct states.
Lunar Eclipse is complete only when every in-scope behaviour is integrated and verified, required inherited suites pass, artifacts install/run cleanly, and no unresolved mandatory failure is concealed. A remaining genuine external gate or approved scoped exception must identify the affected requirement/platform, impact and evidence; it does not count as verified functionality. A worker may not mark the pass complete merely because its allocated task list ended.
LE-15 — Explicit external decisions
Existing Sol Happy commercial/production decisions remain authoritative: undefined subscription lifecycle, retention/grace policy, live service configuration, approved resource budgets and production cutover/spending require their existing approvals. Do not invent them in this pass. Implement enforceable local behaviour, tested entitlement hooks and non-destructive failure states while affected live paths remain visibly blocked. This section adds no new fee, provider, donor or release deadline.

2026-10-09 — APPROVED ASSISTANTS, SPECIALISTS, CONNECT AND INLINE COMMAND REQUIREMENTS
Assistants are persistent configurable conversational identities, distinct from job-defined reusable Specialists. Each Assistant owns multiple persistent conversation threads, with create, rename, switch, search, pin, archive, delete and branch management. Thread history and work context are separate, while Assistant-level memory and permitted cross-thread retrieval are shared. Spaces and Assistants open the same canonical threads and Task/Runs without copying state.
All 9to1 chat services must automatically compact working context while retaining complete original messages and retrievable history, so conversations can continue for months or years without arbitrary message-count caps. Finite model context and resource limitations must be handled honestly; summaries must never replace source history.
Assistants must retain all inherited Agents functionality, with complete feature-parity auditing and user-facing management for identity, instructions, knowledge/files, memory, models, tools/apps, Skills, Quick Actions, permissions, approvals, budgets, queues, delegation, history, background execution, steering, recovery, proactive contact and optional Mini Computer. Support configuration revision history, data lifecycle controls, search, durable artifacts, notifications and concurrent tasks.
Connect is the 9to1 communications app (email, chat and supported calls), not the external integration manager. Assistants and Specialists are selectable addressable contacts. Users can type an Assistant name into an email recipient field or message/call them. Responses stay in the originating channel and thread: email replies to email, chat to chat, calls in calls. The same Assistant identity and authorised work remain accessible in the Assistants app; approvals and notifications may surface separately without moving the primary reply.
Across supported 9to1 composers, @ opens a searchable picker for Assistants, Specialists and supported apps (such as Write and Present). A bare mention is passive and does not execute. An explicitly bounded instruction, for example @Present [Create five slides from this report], is a structured compact INLINE rich-text command, not a separate block editor, card or paragraph. Only that mention and its instruction are specially formatted; surrounding text remains normal, and typing resumes normally after the command. Support multiple commands in one paragraph, wrapping, editing, keyboard accessibility, persistence, copying and canonical identity. Preserve exact boundaries so ordinary text cannot accidentally execute. Commands respect Home permissions, approvals and revocation.
Implement and accept these as complete vertical product features with usable UI, backing behaviour, persistence, integration and real tests, not just architecture or compilation. Preserve existing compliant infrastructure and all earlier specification requirements.

SH-05 — CAKE ID and account services online
Desktop and web MUST use the same CAKE ID, account identity, organisation context and entitlement services. Ordinary users MUST NOT require WordPress accounts.
Authentication MUST preserve the existing secure public-client contract, including the specified browser-based authorisation flow or an explicitly equivalent secure implementation. Clients MUST NOT contain provider credentials, billing secrets or entitlement-signing secrets.
The supported registration, sign-in, sign-out, recovery, profile, session-inspection and session-revocation journeys MUST work against the production backend. Any journey that sends verification or recovery email MUST use a configured delivery service and expose delivery failures honestly.
Any transition from WordPress-linked authentication MUST use verified account mappings and recovery rules. Matching a mutable username MUST NOT transfer account ownership, administrative authority or paid entitlements.
Jacob’s reserved @CroakyJake handle and account-bound free Business feature grant MUST survive the transition. That grant MUST NOT become an exemption from resource accounting, security permissions or third-party spending approval.
Browser applications MUST use authenticated equivalents of Home’s shared services without requiring a local Home installation. Permission approval, trust, revocation and audit semantics MUST remain consistent with native applications.
Personal and organisation contexts MUST remain separate throughout navigation, storage, billing, search and AI access. Switching accounts or organisations MUST NOT expose cached private information from the previous context.
SH-06 — Full browser versions of the applications
Every non-exempt Workspace and AI application MUST have a functional browser version.
The target is the same application on the web, not a companion dashboard, viewer-only edition or simplified alternative. At equivalent viewport sizes, the browser version MUST preserve the desktop application’s information architecture, tools, editor structure, commands, menus, selection behaviour, settings and supported workflows.
Browser-specific adaptations are permitted for actual capability differences and responsive layouts. They MUST NOT justify avoidable feature loss.
Web implementations MUST preserve CUI’s public semantics, shared component contracts, canonical state identities and supported actions. A browser-specific runtime is permitted; an independently redesigned, incompatible UI framework is not the intended outcome.
Each app MUST support its applicable create, open, edit, save, reopen, history, import/export, sharing and recovery operations. The shared contextual AI bar MUST operate on the real semantic artifact through authorised owning-app APIs.
The web inventory MUST include the active Terra-form additions: Link, Prototype, Paths, Replay, Files’ organisation types and Variants in their owning applications. These retain their existing ownership and terminology; they MUST NOT be reorganised into different products for the web implementation.
Each application MUST have a capability matrix identifying supported browser operations, equivalent adaptations and exact remaining restrictions. A restriction MUST identify the missing capability, affected operation, user-visible behaviour and validation evidence.
A desktop-only feature is not sufficient reason to omit an otherwise useful web app. Mini Computer retains its existing web exemption unless the required hosted-compute capability is explicitly provided. Other missing native capabilities MUST NOT be represented as available merely because a browser interface exists.
Direct links, browser refresh, back/forward navigation and account restoration MUST preserve the intended application and artifact context. Unsupported browsers MUST receive a meaningful compatibility state rather than a broken interface.
SH-07 — Files and 9to1 Drive production hosting
9to1 Drive MUST become a real hosted storage service used by the web and desktop applications.
A file uploaded in the browser and opened on desktop MUST retain the same FileID and durable revision history. Local materialisation is a managed replica, not an unrelated imported copy. Files remains responsible for storage and filesystem operations; the owning application remains responsible for semantic document editing and collaboration.
Private file storage MUST remain private. Protected downloads and shares MUST use access-controlled routes that enforce current account, organisation and object permissions. Possession of an object key MUST NOT grant access.
Backblaze B2 is the canonical object-storage backend for 9to1 Drive file bytes and other private hosted objects. Buckets containing private user or deployment data MUST remain private. Direct public bucket/object URLs MUST NOT substitute for protected sharing. Production downloads MUST be mediated by access-controlled 9to1/Cloudflare routes or by narrowly scoped, short-lived signed URLs issued only after the owning service has authorised the request. B2 application keys MUST be least-privilege, scoped to the required bucket/prefix/capabilities, and MUST NOT be embedded in browser or desktop clients.
Transfers MUST have durable identities, resumable progress, cancellation, integrity validation and recoverable failure states. Upload completion MUST not be reported until both content and the authoritative metadata commit have succeeded. Interrupted operations MUST be reconciled without invisible orphan uploads or duplicated quota charges.
Storage enforcement MUST account for committed usage and in-flight reservations. Concurrent uploads MUST NOT overspend the same allocation.
Normal connected synchronisation MUST be push-based and incremental, with durable cursors and replay-safe reconciliation. Polling and full rescans remain recovery mechanisms rather than the ordinary propagation path.
Sharing, search, previews, AI retrieval, version restoration and Trash MUST operate on the same canonical objects and permissions. Restoring an earlier revision MUST preserve subsequent history. Ordinary deletion remains recoverable; permanent purge remains a distinct protected operation.

SH-10 — Cloud AI and connected application services
Cloud-backed features MUST use real provider connections, with credentials held by trusted services.
The AI gateway MUST enforce identity, organisation policy, model entitlement, resource limits and Dust before execution. It MUST support streaming, cancellation, provider failures and recoverable interrupted sessions.
Usage MUST follow the existing reserve → run → settle contract. Parallel requests MUST NOT spend the same balance twice, and uncertain provider outcomes MUST remain subject to reconciliation rather than arbitrary charging or credit creation. Local models and core local tools MUST NOT be charged as cloud AI usage.
Desktop, web and Personal API access MUST draw from the same applicable entitlement and usage services. Personal API access retains its existing eligibility and shared-allocation rules.
Every existing feature that declares an online dependency MUST have that dependency implemented and validated. This includes applicable collaboration, organisation services, provider connections, notifications, Forms responses, published integrations, Agents and Automations.
Execution location MUST be explicit. A browser task, a cloud-hosted task and a task requiring an enrolled desktop device are different capabilities. Closing a tab MUST NOT silently terminate a task advertised as cloud-hosted; an offline device MUST NOT be shown as executing work.
Long-running operations MUST expose durable job identity, progress, cancellation, retries and results. Reconnection MUST NOT repeat consequential actions. Persistent work MUST retain its authorised identity, scope and funding source.
SH-11 — Operations, security and release delivery
The production service MUST include health checks, actionable failure reporting, privacy-preserving diagnostics and alerts for material outages, failed billing processing, failed jobs and approaching resource limits.
Rate limits, account quotas and workload admission controls MUST prevent one customer from consuming another customer’s allocation or exhausting shared services without bounds. Spending alerts MUST NOT be treated as equivalent to an enforced spending ceiling.
Backups and recovery MUST cover canonical metadata, file revisions, account mappings, entitlement records, site source and deployment configuration—not merely a collection of uploaded bytes. Restoration MUST be tested, with documented recovery objectives.
The existing Privacy Ceiling applies to hosted services, provider integrations, telemetry, retention, exports and deletion propagation. Moving functionality online MUST NOT silently broaden AI access or weaken promised encryption.
Deployment pipelines MUST identify exact source revisions, validate changes before activation and support rollback. Database/schema and client updates MUST account for already-open browser sessions and older supported native clients.
Public download and update paths MUST provide real, verified release artifacts. Home and Launcher MUST continue using their shared package authority, integrity checks and staged activation rather than separate manually maintained update lists.
SH-12 — End-to-end acceptance
Acceptance MUST exercise the deployed services, not only mocks or isolated components.

Canvas
Purpose, ownership and boundaries
9-1 Canvas is the handwriting, sketching, drawing and freeform spatial-authoring application in 9to1. Canvas owns Canvas artifacts, spatial composition, page/infinite-canvas geometry, drawing/ink editing, Canvas tool state, Canvas-specific view state and the Canvas domain API.
Canvas is not a Boards replacement and MUST NOT become a generic workspace/page system. Boards owns structured mixed-content workspaces and pages; Canvas owns freeform spatial drawing documents. Boards MAY host a live Canvas artifact, but the embedded Canvas remains owned by Canvas and retains its Canvas ArtifactID.
Canvas MUST use CUI for the visible application shell, menus, toolbars, inspectors, dialogs, launch screen and ordinary controls. A specialised accelerated drawing/rendering surface MAY exist as a CUI control for performance; .cui markup MUST NOT require each stroke sample to become an independent generic UI widget.
Donor and upstream contract
Rnote is the authoritative donor for mature handwriting, drawing, stroke, selection, rendering and applicable import/export behaviour. The implementation agent MUST obtain the latest appropriate stable Rnote source when the Canvas implementation pass begins, record the exact upstream repository, commit/release identifier and licence, and include the selected donor source in the Canvas source tree/build graph in accordance with the global Source & Donor Apps contract.
Canvas MUST maintain a donor-parity manifest generated from inspection of the selected Rnote revision. Every user-visible donor capability MUST be classified as PRESERVE, REPLACE_WITH_9TO1_NATIVE_EQUIVALENT or NOT_APPLICABLE. An unclassified donor feature is a release blocker, not permission to omit it.
* PRESERVE means the donor behaviour, shortcuts, input semantics, quality-of-life behaviour and applicable data behaviour remain available through the 9to1 implementation.
* REPLACE_WITH_9TO1_NATIVE_EQUIVALENT is used when 9to1 already owns the equivalent platform capability, including CUI shell/UI, Dulche AI, Home permission handling, Files storage integration or other shared 9to1 services.
* NOT_APPLICABLE requires a concrete technical, legal or product-boundary reason and validation that its omission does not remove expected Canvas functionality.
Proprietary donor AI MUST NOT be copied. Any applicable AI-assisted behaviour is implemented through Dulche and the Canvas typed API.
Supported platforms and capability negotiation
Canvas MUST ship on every 9to1 platform for which the app is not explicitly exempt under the global platform/web rules. Desktop/native and web implementations MUST share the same Canvas artifact schema, stable identities, domain API semantics and server-side canonical entities.
Platform-specific input or rendering capability differences MUST be negotiated explicitly. Hardware capability absence MUST NOT be misrepresented as format incapability.
* If pressure is unavailable, Canvas records and renders strokes using the declared non-pressure fallback without deleting pressure data already stored in the artifact.
* If tilt, barrel buttons, palm rejection assistance or another device capability is unavailable, the UI MUST disable or omit only the dependent control and expose a capability-unavailable reason where the absence is user-relevant.
* Opening an artifact on a lower-capability platform MUST preserve unsupported stored data for later use on a capable platform.
Canonical artifact model and identity
The native full-fidelity Canvas format is .9to1c. Persisted Canvas data MUST be schema-versioned. Readers MUST migrate, preserve or reject incompatible schema versions explicitly and MUST NOT guess the meaning of unknown fields.
CanvasArtifact {
  ArtifactID: StableID
  SchemaVersion: Version
  RevisionID: RevisionID
  DisplayName: string
  CanvasMode: INFINITE | PAGED
  PageOrder: PageID[]
  SharedResources: ResourceRef[]
  CollaborationMetadata: CollaborationState
  DocumentSettings: CanvasDocumentSettings
}
CanvasPage {
  PageID: StableID
  Bounds: InfiniteBounds | PageBounds
  Background: BackgroundDefinition
  LayerOrder: LayerID[]
  ObjectOrder: ObjectID[]
  RevisionID: RevisionID
}
CanvasObject {
  ObjectID: StableID
  ObjectTypeID: TypeID
  LayerID: LayerID
  Geometry: Geometry
  Transform: Transform
  Style: ObjectStyle
  Accessibility: AccessibilityMetadata
  SharedObjectRef?: SharedObjectReference
  RevisionID: RevisionID
}
InkStroke {
  StrokeID: StableID
  ToolDefinitionID: ToolDefinitionID
  Samples: StrokeSample[]
  ResolvedBrushProperties: BrushProperties
  Transform: Transform
  RevisionID: RevisionID
}
ArtifactID, PageID, LayerID, ObjectID and StrokeID MUST remain stable across rename, move, reorder, zoom, pan, style change and save/reopen. Display names, page positions, z-order and file paths MUST NOT be used as persistent identity.
Document mode and page-type model
Canvas MUST support both INFINITE and PAGED document modes as first-class modes selectable through the top-right quick-settings surface.
* INFINITE mode provides a spatially unbounded working area for normal user workflows and MUST NOT expose an artificial page edge as document structure.
* PAGED mode contains ordered PageID entities with explicit page size, orientation where applicable and page/background settings.
* Page size, orientation, background and page ordering are document state and therefore collaborate, persist and travel with the artifact.
Changing between INFINITE and PAGED is a structural conversion, not a cosmetic toggle. The conversion workflow MUST preview the mapping of existing content, identify content that would cross/clash with generated page boundaries, and require explicit confirmation before committing a conversion that changes layout.
Conversion MUST be undoable/recoverable through document history and MUST NOT clip, discard or rasterise existing objects silently.
Persistence, autosave and recovery
Canvas persistence MUST be atomic at the smallest user-visible document mutation/revision boundary supported by the storage architecture. A partially written resource MUST NOT make the last known-good artifact revision unreadable.
* Autosave MUST persist committed document mutations without requiring a manual Save command.
* A save failure MUST surface an explicit unsaved/error state and retain recoverable local work.
* Crash recovery MUST restore the last durable revision and recover newer journaled/temporary operations where available.
* Imported source files MUST NOT be destructively overwritten merely because they were opened. Overwrite/export requires an explicit user operation appropriate to the source format.
* Closing an artifact while durable persistence is unresolved MUST provide an explicit recovery choice rather than silently discarding changes.

source_text:
Contextual tool-options host
When the active tool exposes contextual options, Canvas MUST render one secondary floating options surface immediately above the primary bottom toolbar. Tool implementations MUST declare their options through a common option schema rather than constructing unrelated private popup systems.
CanvasToolDefinition {
  ToolID: StableToolID
  DisplayName: string
  Icon: IconRef
  Shortcut?: Shortcut
  InputModes: InputMode[]
  Cursor: CursorDefinition
  OptionSchema?: ToolOptionSchema
  CapabilityRequirements: CapabilityID[]
  DomainActionMappings: ActionID[]
}
Selecting a tool activates it. Re-selecting the active tool MUST open/focus its deeper option surface when that tool has options. A long-press or context menu MAY expose secondary actions, but no required capability may exist only behind long-press.
Select and Pan
Select is the canonical object/stroke manipulation tool. It MUST support the applicable Rnote-derived selection modes plus shared-object selection semantics, including single selection, multi-selection and lasso/area selection where supported by the donor/object type.
* Applicable selected content MUST support move, resize, rotate, duplicate, delete/recover, cut/copy/paste, group/ungroup, z-order/layer movement, alignment/distribution where meaningful and lock/unlock.
* An operation unsupported by a selected object type MUST be disabled with a defined capability reason rather than appearing to succeed.
Pan is an explicit navigation tool. Pointer/stylus movement while Pan is active MUST navigate the viewport and MUST NOT create or modify drawing content.
Pen system and preset pens
Pen is the primary structured ink-authoring tool and MUST preserve applicable Rnote pen/brush behaviour. Pen options appear in the contextual tool-options surface above the bottom toolbar.
Canvas MUST ship with useful preset pens derived from the available drawing engines in the selected donor revision. Presets MUST cover the major donor-supported writing/drawing instrument classes that remain applicable, such as ordinary ink/ballpoint-style writing, fountain/variable-width ink, pencil and highlighter/marker behaviour where the donor supports them.
PenPreset {
  PenPresetID: StableID
  Name: string
  ToolEngineID: ToolEngineID
  TipOrNib: NibDefinition
  BaseWidth: Length
  PressureCurve?: Curve
  TiltResponse?: TiltDefinition
  Opacity: number
  Colour: Colour
  Smoothing: SmoothingDefinition
  Stabilisation: StabilisationDefinition
  EngineParameters: Map<string, TypedValue>
  Favourite: boolean
  RevisionID: RevisionID
}
The Pen menu MUST provide a Custom Pen workflow. Users MUST be able to create, preview, save, duplicate, rename, reorder, favourite, edit and delete/recover custom pen presets.
* The custom-pen editor MUST expose only properties supported by the selected ToolEngineID.
* Saving a pen preset MUST NOT retroactively alter existing strokes unexpectedly. Existing strokes retain resolved brush properties or an explicit versioned preset reference sufficient to reproduce their authored appearance.
* Preset and custom pen selection MUST be keyboard and touch accessible.
Eraser
The Eraser tool MUST expose at least two user-facing modes in its contextual options:
* Natural Eraser — drag over drawing content to erase according to the configured donor-supported erasure semantics, including partial/stroke behaviour where provided.
* Quick Eraser — click/tap a target stroke or object to remove the complete resolved target immediately.
Quick Eraser deletion MUST use the same document history/domain delete operation as other Canvas deletion and therefore MUST remain undoable/recoverable. The target-resolution rule MUST be deterministic when objects overlap.
