source_text:
Input, stylus and gesture contract
Input quality is a core Canvas requirement. Canvas MUST preserve applicable high-fidelity stylus information provided by the runtime, including pressure and tilt when available.
* Pen/stylus drawing, touch navigation and mouse/trackpad interaction MUST be distinguishable so ordinary navigation does not create unintended ink.
* Applicable eraser/barrel-button semantics from the selected donor must remain available.
* Palm rejection MUST use platform/donor capabilities where available and MUST fail predictably when hardware/runtime support is absent.
* Pan, zoom and rotate gestures MUST NOT mutate document content unless the active tool/action explicitly maps the gesture to a content mutation.
* Stored pressure/tilt data MUST survive save/reopen and lower-capability viewing even if the current device cannot generate equivalent samples.
Layers, ordering and object manipulation
Canvas MUST preserve applicable Rnote layer functionality. Layers use stable LayerID identities and are document state.
* Users MUST be able to create, rename, reorder, hide/show, lock/unlock and delete/recover layers where supported by the donor model.
* Moving an object between layers changes LayerID membership without changing ObjectID.
* Hidden/locked layers MUST obey the same selection/edit restrictions through UI and API.
Z-order within a layer and layer order are distinct concepts and MUST NOT be conflated by APIs or UI.
Shared Productivity Engine and cross-app object semantics
Canvas MUST use Home's Shared Productivity Engine for every shared object type it supports. Canvas owns spatial placement; the shared engine owns the shared object's semantic content/model.
* Shared rich text, shapes, tables, media, graphs, equations, code, Generative UI and other registered shared objects MUST retain their shared schema when copied, embedded or referenced across supporting 9to1 apps.
* The shared Rnote-derived ink model MUST allow structured ink to remain editable ink in Boards, Present, Write or Spaces where the destination declares ink support.
* Unsupported destination/object combinations MUST fail explicitly or require an explicit user-selected flatten/export operation; silent rasterisation or semantic loss is prohibited.
Clipboard and drag/drop MUST carry a typed multi-representation payload containing stable/source references plus portable shared-object representations as applicable. The destination chooses the highest-fidelity compatible representation; it MUST NOT silently choose a lower-fidelity bitmap when a supported structured representation exists.
Files and Boards integration
Files is authoritative for storage/navigation semantics of Canvas artifacts. Canvas is authoritative for Canvas document semantics.
Boards MUST be able to host a live Canvas artifact/reference. A live Board embed references the same ArtifactID and canonical revision stream rather than creating an unmanaged duplicate.
* Editing an authorised live Canvas embed in Boards edits the canonical Canvas artifact through Canvas domain operations.
* Opening the same ArtifactID in Canvas and Boards MUST resolve to the same underlying artifact.
* A snapshot/static copy is permitted only through an explicit user operation that clearly identifies the result as a copy/export rather than a live embed.
Dulche contextual AI
The bottom-toolbar AI item is the sole normal Canvas entry point for expanding the shared Dulche contextual AI bar. Canvas MUST NOT show a second permanently expanded AI bar while the bottom toolbar is present.
When AI is selected, the shared AI bar floats immediately above the bottom toolbar and the AI toolbar item becomes the selected tool. The bar contains the platform-standard AI access-mode controls, including Read-only and Write modes.
Selecting a different Canvas tool hides the expanded AI bar but MUST NOT automatically cancel an authorised active AI session. AI surface visibility and AI session lifecycle are distinct state.
CanvasAIState {
  SessionID?: StableID
  Lifecycle: NONE | IDLE | ACTIVE | WAITING_FOR_USER | COMPLETED | FAILED
  SurfaceVisibility: HIDDEN | EXPANDED
  IsAIToolSelected: boolean
}
* IsAIToolSelected = true requires SurfaceVisibility = EXPANDED.
* If SurfaceVisibility = HIDDEN and Lifecycle is ACTIVE or WAITING_FOR_USER, Canvas MUST show a compact sparkle session indicator immediately beside the top-right quick-settings pill.
* Clicking the top-right sparkle indicator selects AI, restores the existing SessionID and expands the AI bar above the bottom toolbar. It MUST NOT create a duplicate session.
* If a hidden session completes or fails, the indicator MUST enter a non-intrusive completed/error attention state until inspected/dismissed; it MUST NOT force the AI bar open or steal editing focus.
Dulche MUST receive permission-filtered semantic Canvas context including the active ArtifactID/PageID, stable object/stroke IDs, spatial relationships, text/shared-object semantics, current selection, document revision, current Canvas tool state where relevant and the Canvas actions allowed by the current AI access mode.
* Read-only mode MAY inspect, search, reason, explain, navigate and propose changes but MUST NOT mutate the artifact or editor state.
* Write mode MAY mutate Canvas only through typed Canvas/shared-object actions and the normal revision, permission, undo and conflict model.
* A user reference such as 'these four boxes' MUST resolve to stable target IDs at request/execution binding time. Later selection changes MUST NOT silently retarget the running operation.
* If targeted objects change incompatibly before an AI commit, the operation MUST return a revision/conflict result rather than blindly overwriting newer edits.
Handwriting recognition, OCR or AI-generated descriptions are derived metadata unless the user explicitly invokes a conversion that creates a new typed/text representation. Derived recognition MUST NOT silently replace canonical ink.
Spaces and Automations integration
Spaces MUST be able to open/reference an authorised Canvas artifact and edit it conversationally using 9to1.Canvas typed actions. Spaces MUST NOT use mouse/keyboard simulation when the equivalent Canvas action exists.
Automations MUST receive exhaustive Canvas UI/API parity subject to the same permissions and platform capabilities. Canvas MUST publish typed events for meaningful document changes and MUST NOT flood workflows with raw pointer-move events.
Minimum automatable event families:
* Artifact opened/closed/saved/recovered.
* Page created/deleted/reordered and document mode changed.
* Object/stroke created/changed/deleted.
* Layer created/changed/deleted/reordered.
* Shared object inserted/changed/removed.
* Collaboration/revision conflict and recovery state changes that are meaningful for automation.
Collaboration and conflict semantics
Canvas collaboration MUST operate on canonical structured document entities rather than exchanging flattened screenshots or whole-document last-write-wins blobs.
* Concurrent edits to independent strokes/objects/pages SHOULD merge without destroying unrelated work.
* Conflicting edits to the same canonical entity MUST be detected using revision/operation semantics and resolved deterministically or surfaced as a conflict.
* Naive timestamp last-write-wins MUST NOT be the default conflict strategy.
* Remote cursors, selections and transient viewport positions are collaboration presence/session state and MUST NOT alter canonical document content.
The implementation MAY use CRDTs, operation logs or another maintainable internal algorithm provided the observable collaboration, revision and recovery contract is satisfied.
Undo, redo and history
All ordinary Canvas document mutations initiated by UI, AI, Spaces or Automation MUST enter the same canonical history/revision system unless an operation explicitly declares non-document session state.
* Undo/redo MUST operate on semantic user-visible operations, not arbitrary internal rendering steps.
* AI/API mutations MUST be attributable in history/audit metadata.
* Undoing deletion restores the same stable object/stroke identity where restoration semantics permit it.
* Structural mode conversion, bulk manipulation and imported-content insertion MUST be represented as coherent reversible operations or explicit multi-operation transactions.
Import and export
The native .9to1c format is authoritative for full-fidelity Canvas behaviour. Canvas MUST retain all applicable Rnote import/export capabilities from the selected donor revision in addition to 9to1-native integrations.
Import/export MUST preserve supported structured content and MUST produce an explicit compatibility report when the source or destination cannot represent part of the native Canvas model.
* Unsupported features MUST be classified as translated, degraded, omitted or blocked with the affected entity identified.
* Silent loss of layers, stroke properties, page structure, shared objects, accessibility metadata or other canonical content is prohibited.
* A successful file creation/open is not sufficient validation; representative round trips MUST compare semantic content.
Accessibility
Canvas MUST make ordinary authoring and document-management workflows operable by keyboard and assistive technology even though the primary document is spatial/visual.
* All toolbar, menu, submenu, quick-settings, document-pill and AI controls require accessible names, roles, focus states and keyboard operation.
* Meaningful Canvas objects MUST be inspectable through an accessible structured object/list view exposing object name/type, authored text, alt description and relevant ordering/spatial relationship information.
* Visual objects MUST support alt text/description where appropriate.
* Pure freehand ink is not required to become authoritative text automatically. AI/OCR descriptions MUST remain clearly derived metadata unless the user explicitly adopts/converts them.
* Required state MUST NOT be communicated only by colour; focus must be visible; zoom/display scaling and reduced-motion preferences must be respected.
Security and permissions
Canvas inherits Home's permission broker and global API permission model. Canvas MUST declare action risk classifications and MUST NOT bypass Home for protected external or destructive operations.
* Opening a Canvas file MUST NOT grant embedded code, Generative UI, media or linked artifacts arbitrary filesystem/network/account access.
* Embedded/shared objects execute only within the permissions of their owning capability/runtime.
* Untrusted imported Canvas content MUST NOT change Home trust grants, security policy or sandbox restrictions.
* Whole-artifact permanent deletion is routed through Files' canonical deletion semantics; ordinary object/stroke deletion remains Canvas document history unless explicitly made permanent through an authorised action.
Typed Canvas API
Canvas MUST expose a versioned first-party API namespace with UI parity. The canonical namespace is 9to1.Canvas; language bindings that cannot use 9to1 literally use the global aliasing rule without changing canonical action names.
CanvasMutationRequest {
  BaseRevisionID: RevisionID
  OperationID: StableID
  ActorContext: PermissionFilteredActorContext
}
CanvasMutationResult {
  RevisionID: RevisionID
  ChangedIDs: StableID[]
  Warnings: Warning[]
}
Required action families include:
* Artifact: Create, Open, Get, Rename, Save/Flush, Close, Recover, GetRevisionHistory, RestoreRevision and document-settings operations.
* Pages: List, Get, Create, Duplicate, Move/Reorder, Delete/Restore, SetBounds/Size/Orientation and set page/background properties.
* Layers: List, Create, Rename, Reorder, SetVisibility, SetLocked, MoveObjects, Delete/Restore.
* Objects/Strokes: query/get, insert/create, update style, transform, duplicate, group/ungroup, reorder, move layer, delete/restore and semantic search.
* Ink: begin/append/end stroke for authorised input/runtime integrations, create from structured samples, update allowed stroke properties and query stroke geometry/metadata.
* Pens: ListPresets, CreatePreset, DuplicatePreset, UpdatePreset, Delete/RestorePreset and favourite/reorder operations.
* Insert/shared objects: enumerate registered Canvas-compatible types and create each through its canonical shared-object action.
* Import/export: enumerate formats/capabilities, start long-running import/export jobs, query status, cancel and retrieve CompatibilityReport.
* AI/session integration: semantic-context queries and session binding/status operations; AI model execution remains owned by the shared Dulche platform.
* Collaboration: presence/query, comments if Canvas exposes them, share/reference state and conflict/revision operations consistent with the owning collaboration service.
Actions that enumerate unbounded collections MUST paginate/stream. Long-running import/export/render work MUST return JobID, status and cancellation. Retry-safe mutations MUST use OperationID idempotency.
Typed errors MUST distinguish at least NOT_FOUND, INVALID_ARGUMENT, PERMISSION_DENIED, REVISION_CONFLICT, CAPABILITY_UNAVAILABLE, UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE, FORMAT_INCOMPATIBLE, IO_ERROR, RUNTIME_ERROR and CANCELLED.
Performance and resource constraints
Canvas MUST remain responsive for realistically large documents and MUST NOT render/process the entire spatial document every frame solely because it exists.
* Viewport rendering MUST use spatial culling/virtualisation and appropriate caching so distant off-screen objects do not impose per-frame work proportional to total document size.
* Incremental edits such as adding one stroke SHOULD avoid rewriting/re-rendering unrelated content where the persistence/rendering architecture can preserve correctness without doing so.
* Caches MUST be bounded and invalidated by semantic revisions rather than growing without limit.
* Large images/media MUST use progressive/appropriate decoding and MUST NOT block the interactive input loop unnecessarily.
The implementation test suite MUST include large-canvas fixtures with high stroke/object counts, embedded images/shared objects and widely separated spatial extents. Performance claims require measured runtime evidence on the declared supported-hardware baseline; 'feels fast' is not acceptance evidence.
Failure and recovery behaviour
* If a shared object renderer fails, Canvas MUST preserve the object data and show a typed recoverable error representation rather than deleting or flattening it.
* If a donor tool/backend capability fails to initialise, Canvas MUST report the unavailable capability and keep unaffected tools usable.
* Transient save/sync failures MUST use bounded retry/backoff and expose unresolved state; infinite retries are prohibited.
* If collaboration connectivity is lost, local permitted editing MAY continue when the storage/conflict model supports it, but unsynchronised state MUST be visible and reconciliation MUST use revision/conflict rules on reconnect.
* If an import is partially parseable, Canvas MUST follow the declared import policy: either commit an explicitly reported partial result as a new artifact or fail atomically. It MUST NOT silently present a partial result as full-fidelity success.
Release acceptance criteria
Canvas is release-conformant only when behavioural evidence proves the complete agreed interaction model, donor parity and cross-app integration. Source presence, screenshots, disconnected controls or a successful build alone are insufficient.
The release validation suite MUST demonstrate at minimum:
* Create an INFINITE artifact, draw/write with pressure-capable test input, pan/zoom, select/manipulate objects, save, close and reopen with stable IDs and stroke properties preserved.
* Create a PAGED artifact, configure size/orientation/background, add/reorder pages and save/reopen.
* Convert between document modes through the preview/confirmation workflow without silent clipping/loss and verify undo/recovery.
* Bottom toolbar layout/order, selected-tool name, hover/focus tooltips and contextual options above the toolbar.
* Preset Pen use plus create/edit/save/duplicate/reorder/delete/recover Custom Pen workflows.
* Natural Eraser and Quick Eraser, including deterministic overlap targeting and undo.
* Insert cascading menu with Text, Shapes, Media, Table and Other; verify Text Box/Heading/Paragraph, shape/line catalogue, Image/Audio/Video, shared Table and Graph under Other.
* Verify Drawing is not exposed as a redundant Insert item.
* Shared-object parity tests proving Canvas does not substitute reduced private Text/Shape/Media/Table/Graph implementations.
* Top-right quick-settings pill with page type, background and Smart Pen plus correct document-vs-user persistence scope.
* Smart Pen creates neater structured ink, does not convert to typed text and restores exact pre-adjustment content through undo.
* AI selected -> shared floating Dulche bar appears above toolbar; changing tool hides the bar without cancelling an active session; active hidden session shows the top-right sparkle indicator; clicking that indicator restores the same SessionID.
* Read-only AI is unable to mutate; Write AI performs a real typed edit and respects revision conflict if targets change.
* Live Canvas embed in Boards edits the same ArtifactID, and an explicitly created snapshot produces a distinct copy.
* Files rename/move does not change ArtifactID; Files delete/recovery semantics work for the whole artifact.
* Spaces performs a semantic Canvas edit through the Canvas API without UI simulation.
* Automation/API parity for representative page, layer, stroke, shared-object, pen, settings, import/export and recovery operations.
* Cross-app clipboard fidelity for structured ink and at least two supported shared-object types with Boards plus at least one of Write/Present.
* Concurrent editing on independent objects preserves both edits; conflicting same-entity edits produce deterministic merge/conflict behaviour rather than silent last-write-wins loss.
* Keyboard-only operation of required shell/menu/tool workflows and assistive-technology inspection of meaningful Canvas objects.
* Representative Rnote donor-parity suite against the pinned donor manifest, with every manifest entry evidenced or explicitly accepted as a scoped exception.
* Native and web/open-on-lower-capability round trips preserve unsupported pressure/tilt and other stored data.
* Crash/interrupted-save recovery from a last-known-good revision plus recoverable newer work.
* Large-canvas stress fixtures demonstrate bounded memory/cache behaviour, viewport culling and acceptable measured pointer/pan/zoom responsiveness on the declared baseline.
Any acceptance path that silently drops user data, silently flattens a supported structured object, reports a disconnected UI control as working, creates duplicate canonical artifacts during live embedding, loses a running AI session solely because its UI is hidden, or omits an unreviewed donor feature MUST block release conformance.

source_text:
Planner
Product role and boundary
9-1 Planner is the CUI calendar, schedule, countdown and assignment-planning app. It answers when something happens, when something is due, what the user needs to do, and which canonical 9to1 entities are connected to that plan. Planner is not Home Events, which is an ecosystem activity/history timeline; it is not Spaces Tasks, which represent goal-oriented agentic work/runs; and it is not Automations, which own recurring/event/condition-triggered execution.
Planner MUST expose local/native planning and provider-backed calendar/task data through one coherent typed model without duplicating canonical external or 9to1 entities. References to routes, Mail, Files, Write, Present, Boards, Canvas, Data, Spaces, Automations and other supported entities retain the owning entity's stable identity.
Donor and upstream contract
Planner is a first-party CUI surface. No external application donor is currently normative for Planner. Implementers MUST NOT silently choose a donor and allow donor-specific storage or behaviour to become public Planner authority. Mature calendar standards, provider APIs and the shared 9to1 frameworks MAY be used as implementation references where they do not contradict this specification.
Primary views and navigation
Planner MUST provide Today, Day, Week, Month, Agenda and Tasks views. The main calendar views use conventional direct manipulation: selecting a time range can create an item, timed items can be moved/resized where permitted, all-day items have a dedicated region, overlapping items remain legible, the current-time indicator is visible where relevant, and keyboard navigation can move through dates/items without requiring pointer input.
The sidebar MUST expose the user's calendars/task lists plus three optional modules — Schedule, Countdown and Assignments. Each optional module can be enabled, hidden and reordered by the user. Hiding a module removes its navigation surface only; it MUST NOT delete its data.
Agenda
Agenda is Planner's chronological list of upcoming planning items rather than a time-grid view. It MUST group and order upcoming events and other relevant due/scheduled Planner entities by date/time while preserving each item's canonical identity.
Agenda SHOULD surface at least events, scheduled PlannerTasks and Assignment deadlines. It MAY surface other Planner milestones such as selected Countdowns when the user has enabled that integration. Filters can narrow the list by calendar/list, completion/status, category and other applicable typed fields.
Canonical entity model
Planner's canonical entity families are:
* Calendar — organisation/source container for events, with stable CalendarID, display metadata, ownership/provider binding, capability state and revision metadata.
* PlannerEvent — a time-bounded or all-day event with stable EventID.
* PlannerTask — a personal planning/to-do item with stable PlannerTaskID; this is distinct from Spaces/Dulche TaskID.
* Reminder — a notification rule/state attached to an Event, PlannerTask, Assignment, Countdown or other supported Planner entity.
* RecurrenceDefinition and recurrence exceptions — a versioned repeating-series contract.
* Schedule and ScheduleItem — optional structured day-plan entities.
* Countdown — optional user-defined target-date/time entity.
* Assignment and AssignmentItem — optional structured deadline/work-completion entities.
Display names, sidebar order and current view state are not identities. Stable IDs survive rename, move, reorder, view changes and provider resynchronisation where the provider preserves identity.
PlannerEvent
PlannerEvent MUST contain at least EventID, CalendarID, Title, Description?, Start/End or all-day date span, TimeZone semantics, Location?, Recurrence?, References[], Reminders[], Status, CreatedAt, ModifiedAt, owner/scope, source/provider metadata and revision. Provider-backed events additionally retain the provider's stable event identity/version token where available.
An Event may reference a meeting, Maps route, Files/Write/Present/Board/Canvas/Data artifact, Mail thread/message, Space, Automation output or other registered 9to1 entity. Referencing an entity MUST NOT duplicate its canonical payload.
PlannerTask
PlannerTask MUST contain at least PlannerTaskID, Title, Description?, Status, TaskListID?, DueAt/date?, ScheduledStart?, ScheduledEnd?, Recurrence?, Priority?, References[], Reminders[], CreatedAt, ModifiedAt, owner/scope and revision.
A PlannerTask can be due without being scheduled. Scheduling a PlannerTask onto the calendar assigns ScheduledStart/ScheduledEnd to the same PlannerTaskID; Planner MUST NOT manufacture a duplicate Event merely to render the task in a time-grid.
Dragging an unscheduled task onto a calendar schedules it. Removing it from the time-grid may clear the scheduled window without deleting the task or its due date. Completing/reopening the task preserves its identity/history.
Time zones, all-day values and daylight saving
Timed Event/Task values MUST use real timezone-aware semantics. Planner distinguishes the authoritative event timezone, absolute instant(s), viewer timezone and an explicitly supported floating/local-time representation. A user travelling or changing device timezone MUST NOT silently change the intended meaning of the event.
All-day items are date-based and MUST NOT drift onto an adjacent date through UTC conversion. Recurrence across daylight-saving transitions uses timezone database rules rather than fixed UTC offsets.
Recurrence and occurrence identity
Recurring Events, PlannerTasks, Assignments and Countdowns MUST use a recurrence definition rather than pre-creating an unbounded list of copies. Supported recurrence semantics include the normal daily/weekly/monthly/yearly interval patterns, selected weekdays, end date and occurrence count where applicable.
Each expanded occurrence has stable occurrence identity derived from its series plus occurrence key/date-time. Editing a repeating item MUST support the applicable scopes This occurrence, This and following, and Entire series. A modified/skipped occurrence is stored as an exception; modifying one occurrence MUST NOT flatten the entire series into unrelated records.
The runtime expands only the requested/visible/query interval plus bounded prefetch. Infinite recurrence MUST never be materialised eagerly.
Reminders and Home notifications
Planner reminder delivery uses Home's shared notification service rather than a private Planner notification runtime. An entity MAY own multiple reminder rules such as at start, relative minutes/hours/days before, or a custom trigger supported by the reminder contract.
Reminder runtime state distinguishes at least Scheduled, Fired, Snoozed and Dismissed. Snoozing a reminder changes reminder state/next notification time and MUST NOT rewrite the Event/Task/Assignment's actual start or due time. Recurring-series reminders are evaluated per occurrence.

source_text:
Optional sidebar module: Assignments
Assignment represents structured homework, coursework, project/team work, revision deliverables or similar deadline-based work that needs richer completion tracking than a simple PlannerTask. Assignment has stable AssignmentID, Title, Description?, Status, StartDate?, DueAt/date?, CompletedAt?, Priority?, Category/Course/Project metadata?, owner/scope, Assignees/RelevantPeople, RequiredItems[], OptionalItems[], References[], Reminders[], AutomationRefs[] and revision.
AssignmentItem has stable AssignmentItemID, AssignmentID, parent/nesting relationship?, title/description, Required/Optional classification, completion/progress state, optional weight, optional assignee and revision. Required and optional items remain distinguishable in UI, API, Automations and completion rules.
Assignment progress and completion
Assignments MUST support partial completion rather than only Done/Not Done. Required statuses include at least Not Started, In Progress, Completed and Cancelled; overdue is derived from the due date versus completion state and MUST be queryable even if represented visually as a status badge.
Progress MAY be automatically calculated from required items, manually set for work that cannot be represented as a checklist, or calculated using explicit item weights. Equal weighting is the default only when no weights are supplied. Optional items do not prevent formal completion.
By default, an Assignment cannot be marked Completed while required items remain incomplete. A user may explicitly override that rule where permitted, with a visible warning/impact confirmation. Automation/API calls must make an equivalent override explicit rather than silently bypassing required items.
Assignment views MUST include useful states such as Due soon, Overdue, In progress, Completed and All, with filters/grouping such as due date, course/project/team, priority and assignee where data exists.
Team assignments
Assignments MAY have an owner, assignees/contributors and item-level assignees. Being named as an assignee or relevant person does not itself grant edit permission; normal sharing/ACL state remains authoritative.
Assignment-level completion can aggregate item work across people while preserving who completed/changed each item where audit/history is available.
Assignment Automations and extension workflows
Planner exposes Assignment events/state to Automations, but Planner itself MUST NOT secretly send external communications as a built-in overdue side effect. A user may create an Automation such as: when an Assignment becomes overdue and is incomplete, draft or send a Mail extension request to the relevant person.
The workflow boundary is strict: Planner owns Assignment state; Automations owns trigger/condition execution; Mail owns sending. Automatic external sending requires the applicable authorised Mail permission/trust grant and remains subject to the global external-side-effect/risk model.
Useful Assignment event families include AssignmentCreated, AssignmentUpdated, AssignmentProgressChanged, AssignmentDueSoon, AssignmentOverdue, AssignmentCompleted, AssignmentReopened and item-completion events. Automations can query DueAt, Status, Progress, RequiredItems, OptionalItems, assignees and references through typed Planner APIs.
Cross-app typed references
Planner references MUST use the owning app's canonical stable IDs and permissions. A referenced artifact may render a preview/embedded surface only through the owning app's declared reference/embed contract.
If a referenced entity is unavailable, revoked or deleted, the Planner item remains valid and surfaces the reference as unavailable/broken; Planner MUST NOT delete the Event/Task/Assignment simply because one attachment/reference disappeared.

source_text:
Persistence, sync, history and recovery
Planner native state is versioned and crash-safe. Calendar/Event/PlannerTask/Assignment/Schedule/Countdown changes use revision-aware mutations; partial failure must not leave a recurrence series or Assignment hierarchy half-updated.
Normal deletion is recoverable where the entity/storage provider supports recovery. Permanent purge is explicit/high-risk. Provider-backed deletion/recovery follows provider capability while preserving local audit/sync state.
Offline/reconnect queues MUST preserve operation identity/idempotency. Provider conflicts and concurrent same-entity edits surface deterministic merge/conflict state rather than silently overwriting one revision.
Permissions and risk
Read, edit, share/admin, provider/external-side-effect and destructive scopes remain distinct. Having a Planner item in view does not grant permission to mutate its referenced artifact, invite attendees, send Mail or operate a connected provider beyond the caller's authorised capabilities.
Invitation/cancellation sending, external Mail extension requests, provider sharing changes, permanent purge and destructive bulk changes retain their target action's elevated risk/approval requirements.
Accessibility
Planner MUST be keyboard-operable across calendar grids, Agenda, task/assignment lists, Schedule and Countdown. Time-grid cells/items expose meaningful accessible date/time labels; current item/progress and overdue state cannot be conveyed by colour alone.
Screen readers MUST be able to identify item type, title, date/time/due state, recurrence and applicable progress. Schedule percentages and countdown values require textual equivalents. Reduced motion and scalable text/layout follow the global CUI accessibility contract.
Platform capability behaviour
Planner MUST provide useful supported native behaviour on Windows and 9to1-OS plus a useful web version under the global web contract. All clients operate on the same canonical Planner/provider entities.
Native clients MAY have richer OS notification/calendar integration; web may depend on browser notification/background constraints. Capability differences are explicit and MUST NOT silently downgrade the canonical planning state or turn the web app into a read-only viewer.
Performance and resource behaviour
Calendar range queries load only the visible/requested interval plus bounded prefetch; recurring-series expansion is interval-bounded. Large Agenda/task/Assignment lists MUST virtualise. Provider change feeds and shared indexes update incrementally rather than repeatedly refetching all calendars/items.
Schedule live-progress and Countdown ticking MUST update efficiently without causing full Planner-tree rerenders each second. Background timers should coalesce/update at the precision actually visible to the user.
Failure behaviour
Planner MUST return structured failures for EventNotFound, PlannerTaskNotFound, AssignmentNotFound, ScheduleNotFound, CountdownNotFound, InvalidRecurrence, InvalidTimeZone, RevisionConflict, PermissionDenied, ProviderCapabilityUnsupported, ProviderSyncConflict, ReferenceUnavailable, ReminderUnavailable and ImportUnsupportedConstruct, plus the global error contract.
If Home notification/shared services are unavailable, Planner preserves canonical planning state and surfaces notification/reconnect limitations rather than losing Events/Tasks/Assignments. Provider outages preserve queued/retryable state with explicit sync status.
Acceptance requirements
Planner is implementation-complete only when acceptance coverage verifies at least:
* Today, Day, Week, Month, Agenda and Tasks views operate on persisted canonical Planner entities and survive restart.
* Agenda lists upcoming Events/scheduled tasks/Assignment deadlines chronologically without duplicating their underlying identities.
* Scheduling/unscheduling a PlannerTask changes its scheduled window without creating/deleting a duplicate Event.
* Timezone, all-day and daylight-saving tests preserve intended event meaning across viewer/device timezone changes.
* Recurring series support occurrence/this-and-following/whole-series edits, exceptions and bounded expansion.
* Reminders route through Home notifications and snoozing does not rewrite the item's canonical time.
* Schedule can be enabled as an optional sidebar module and shows live elapsed/remaining time plus percentage elapsed/remaining for the current item.
* Countdown can be enabled as an optional sidebar module, supports standalone and linked targets, and linked targets update without duplicated dates.
* Assignments can be enabled as an optional sidebar module and persist partial progress, required/optional items, nested/weighted items where configured, due state, team assignments and completion rules.
* An overdue Assignment can trigger an authorised Automation that drafts/sends a Mail extension request without Planner bypassing Mail/Automation permission rules.
* Maps routes, Mail threads and Files/Write/Present/Boards/Canvas/Data/Space/Automation outputs remain canonical typed references when attached to Planner items.
* Provider calendars capability-negotiate recurrence/attendees/reminders/etc. and synchronise without silent last-write-wins conflict loss.
* iCalendar import/export round-trips representable recurrence/timezone data and reports unsupported constructs.
* The persistent AI bar reads/writes Planner only through permission-filtered semantic context and typed Planner actions.
* Windows, 9to1-OS and web preserve the same canonical entity model while surfacing declared capability differences.
* Large calendar ranges/lists/recurrences remain responsive through bounded expansion, incremental sync/indexing and virtualisation.
* When Home is absent at process start, Planner follows the global Install Home/bootstrap contract rather than launching an incompatible private runtime.

source_text:
Forms
Product role and runtime principle
9-1 Forms is the native CUI structured form, assessment, data-entry and lightweight interactive-application builder. It covers surveys, questionnaires, applications, registrations, feedback, quizzes/tests, database-entry interfaces, conversational interviews, live multiplayer quizzes and custom event-driven experiences while keeping simple forms fast to create.
The canonical result is a structured FormProject and runtime configuration, not a collection of rendered pages. Fields, pages, themes, logic, marking rules, timers, multiplayer state, Data bindings and custom mode behaviour remain typed editable state. The same semantic model is used by the builder, published runtime, AI, Automations and APIs.
Forms MUST support simple no-code creation without exposing advanced complexity by default, but the product ceiling MUST NOT be limited to the capabilities of conventional survey builders. Advanced logic, layout, assessment and multiplayer features use the same underlying canonical objects rather than separate incompatible modes.
Canonical project model
FormProject has stable FormID, ModeDefinition, FormVersions[], Pages[], Fields[], Components[], Theme, LogicGraphID where used, DataBindings[], MarkingScheme, QuestionBanks[], PublishingSettings, AccessPolicy, RuntimeSettings, CreatedAt, ModifiedAt and Revision.
Page/Section objects have stable PageID, ordered child components/fields, layout configuration, visibility rules and Revision. Field has stable FieldID, FieldType, label/help/content, response schema, required/validation state, appearance/layout state, marking configuration where applicable, Data binding where applicable and Revision.
Choice options, table columns, rubric criteria, marking rules, grading schemes, branching rules and reusable components have stable identity when independently addressable. Published runtime and stored responses reference IDs, not question text or screen coordinates.
Builder workspace and preview
The default builder provides a structured page/canvas editor, field/component palette, contextual Inspector, logic/mode controls, theme/layout controls and Preview/Test. Common tasks MUST NOT require the node editor.
Preview supports desktop, tablet, mobile and narrow embedded layouts. Interactive preview can simulate answers, validate branching, exercise marking rules, test Data bindings with safe test context and identify unreachable pages/conditions before publication.
Builder and preview operate on the same canonical FormProject. Preview MUST NOT create a separate approximation that can diverge from published behaviour.
Core field and component types
Forms supports at least short text, long text, number/decimal/currency, email, phone, date/time, duration, single choice, multiple choice, dropdown, checkbox/set, rating/scale, ranking, matrix/grid, file upload, signature where supported, person/reference picker, Data foreign-key lookup, rich text/content, image/media block, calculated/read-only field, hidden/system field, mathematical response, graph response, repeating group and table input.
Field types define canonical answer schemas rather than coercing everything to text. Validation, Data binding and marking consume the typed answer model.
Custom/reusable Form Components may contain multiple child fields and layout/logic, for example Address, Person details, Emergency contact or Rating + comment. Reusing a component preserves structured child identity rather than pasting an opaque widget.
Table input and repeating structured responses
Forms MUST provide a real TableInput field, not merely a multiple-choice grid. TableInput defines typed columns, optional fixed rows, respondent-added rows, minimum/maximum row count, required columns, per-cell/row validation, calculated columns, dropdown/reference columns, duplicate rules and Data bindings.
A table input may write multiple related Data records rather than serialising an entire table into one string. For example an expense report may submit one parent Report record plus one related Expense record per entered row.
Repeating groups provide similar semantics for card/form layouts where each repeated item has multiple fields. TableInput and repeating groups preserve stable row/item identity within a response.
Native modes: Form, Test and Quiz
Forms ships at least three first-party runtime presets built on the common Forms state/marking engine.
Form mode accepts any valid answer according to field validation. It is intended for surveys, applications, registration, feedback and general data collection. Correct/incorrect semantics are absent unless a field explicitly defines assessment behaviour.
Test mode supports correct/incorrect/partial answers, points, marking rules, grading schemes and result release. Respondents normally complete the assessment as a whole and receive score/grade/feedback according to configured release policy.
Quiz mode uses the same assessment engine but supports question-by-question evaluation/progression. After each answer the runtime may show correct/incorrect/partial state, explanation/feedback and then advance according to mode settings. A final score/grade can still be produced.
Mode semantics MUST be expressed through the common runtime/state system rather than three independent engines.
Custom modes and state-machine runtime
Advanced authors can create Custom Modes using the shared node/state system. A custom mode can define start state, question/component selection, timers, score variables, lives/attempts, branching, dialogue turns, participant state, completion conditions and result calculation.
Examples include 'answer three questions correctly as quickly as possible', adaptive difficulty, limited-lives games, interview/conversation flows, staged applications and game-show experiences.
Built-in Form/Test/Quiz behaviour SHOULD be representable as first-party presets over the same runtime concepts so custom modes do not fork core response, Data, accessibility or publishing infrastructure.
Marking engine and multiple accepted answers
Assessable fields support one or more typed MarkingRules. Rules can resolve Correct, Incorrect, Partial, NeedsReview or another configured outcome and award points according to explicit scoring policy.
Text questions can define multiple accepted correct answers. Normalised matching can optionally ignore case, trim/collapse whitespace, normalise Unicode and ignore selected punctuation/diacritics according to author settings.
Example: a question asking for the name of the central processor may accept 'CPU' and 'Central Processing Unit' as equivalent accepted answers without requiring AI.
Rules can be combined with explicit boolean logic such as AcceptedAnswer(A) OR AcceptedAnswer(B) OR Regex(C), and more complex marking flows can use the node editor where appropriate.
Regex validation and marking
Regex is supported for both response validation and marking. Authors can configure pattern, flags, explanatory label and accepted/rejected test cases.
The builder MUST include a regex tester with live example inputs, invalid-pattern diagnostics and clear indication of full-match versus partial-match semantics. Forms MUST NOT execute unbounded or unsafe regex behaviour in a way that can freeze the runtime; implementations use bounded/safe regex execution appropriate to the platform.
Regex rules remain inspectable structured MarkingRule/ValidationRule objects and can be combined with other deterministic rules.
AI, human and hybrid marking
Question-level AI marking can be enabled explicitly. AI marking uses a structured rubric with expected concepts/criteria, maximum points, optional sample correct/partial/incorrect answers, required/forbidden concepts and feedback policy. The result records awarded points, matched/missed criteria, feedback and uncertainty/review state rather than only an opaque prose verdict.
Marking mode may be deterministic automatic, mathematical/symbolic, AI, manual human or hybrid. Hybrid workflows can let deterministic rules resolve obvious answers, invoke AI for unresolved open responses and optionally require human moderation before release.
A useful default marking pipeline is deterministic accepted-answer/regex rules, then mathematical equivalence where applicable, then AI rubric evaluation only when configured and still unresolved. Authors can override this ordering.
QuestionResult records marking provenance so consequential results can show whether a mark came from exact rule, regex, symbolic maths evaluator, AI, human marker or combination.
Partial credit, grading and feedback
Assessments support points, weighted questions, partial credit, criterion/rubric scoring, optional penalties where explicitly configured and section/category subtotals.
GradingScheme maps score/percentage or configured measures to grade/band/pass state. Boundaries are structured editable rules rather than hard-coded labels.
Feedback can be configured per answer/rule/rubric criterion and released immediately, after a question, after submission, after manual review or at a configured release state.
LaTeX and visual mathematics editor
Forms MUST provide first-class mathematical authoring. MathExpression uses LaTeX-compatible canonical representation but can be edited through a visual equation editor so authors/respondents are not required to know LaTeX.
The editor supports fractions, powers/indices, roots, logarithms, trigonometry, calculus notation, sigma/product notation, vectors, matrices, inequalities, sets, piecewise expressions, probability/statistics notation, Greek/special symbols and aligned expressions where supported.
Visual and LaTeX modes edit the same expression and remain bidirectionally synchronised. Invalid LaTeX produces an explicit recoverable editing error rather than losing the prior valid expression.
MathAnswer types include numeric, algebraic expression, equation, inequality, interval, coordinate, vector, matrix, set, multiple expressions and free-working response. Numeric rules can configure exact value, absolute/percentage tolerance, significant figures, decimal places and units where applicable.
Graph plotter and graph-response questions
Forms MUST include a native mathematical graph plotter/editor for quiz/test content. Authors can define functions, equations, inequalities, points, coordinate tables, regions, axes, grid/domain/range configuration and other supported 2D graph primitives.
GraphResponse questions can ask respondents to place points, draw a line/curve, submit coordinates, enter a function/equation for plotting, identify a region or manipulate an existing graph according to declared tools.
Graph answers remain structured GraphDefinition/GraphResponse data, not screenshots. Marking compares the submitted mathematical/graph representation using configured tolerances/equivalence rules where supported.
MathExpression, GraphDefinition and related primitives SHOULD be reusable shared mathematical objects across Forms, Write, Present and other 9to1 surfaces rather than privately reinvented.
Question banks, randomisation, attempts and timing
Forms supports reusable QuestionBank objects with tags, subject/topic, difficulty, points, marking rules and other metadata. A Test/Quiz can select deterministic or random subsets subject to constraints such as minimum questions from specified categories.
Question/choice order can be randomised per participant where configured. Attempts can be unlimited, fixed-count, one-only or custom-mode controlled. Retry policies may target only incorrect questions.
Timing supports whole-assessment timers, per-question/per-section timers, countdowns, time bonus/penalty, late-submission policy and custom timer variables. Server-authoritative timing is required for multiplayer and integrity-sensitive modes.

Publishing, versions and response compatibility
Forms has explicit Draft and Published runtime versions. Editing Draft MUST NOT mutate the currently published experience until the author publishes/activates the new version according to policy.
Every response records FormID and the FormVersionID/schema revision answered. Historical responses remain interpretable even when fields are renamed, moved, hidden or removed in later versions.
Publishing states include at least Draft, Published/Accepting responses and Closed, with optional scheduled open/close where the platform supports it. Authors configure whether in-progress respondents remain on the version they started or migrate only through explicitly safe rules.
Response model, save/resume and editing
Response has stable ResponseID, FormID/FormVersionID, responder/participant identity where known, Answer records keyed by FieldID, started/submitted timestamps, attachments, state, score/marking result where applicable, Data-write status and Revision.
Forms supports configurable draft/save-and-resume, edit-after-submit policy, response limits, duplicate-prevention policy and confirmation/next-action behaviour.
Historical answer values MUST remain attached to the field/version schema that produced them rather than being reinterpreted based only on the latest field label.

source_text:
Automations
Product role and execution boundary
9-1 Automations is the ecosystem-wide workflow-definition and orchestration app. It owns Automation definitions, triggers, control flow, durable execution state and Run history. It does not reimplement the business logic of target apps: every app/device/provider/third-party action executes through the canonical typed action exposed by its owning capability and retains that capability's permissions, risk classification, result/error schema, idempotency semantics and audit trail.
Home owns the shared Node Graph Framework and permission/trust broker. Automations owns Automation entities and orchestration semantics. Dulche executes AI/model/Agent work. Target 9to1 apps, connected services, third-party apps and devices execute their registered typed actions. Raw mouse/keyboard UI automation is non-conformant where a typed action exists.
Landing page: Home and Library
The Automations landing surface has two primary sections: Home and Library.
* Home is an operational dashboard. It surfaces recent runs, currently running/waiting workflows, failures/Needs Attention, upcoming scheduled triggers, permission/connection problems, commonly used Automations and concise execution-health information.
* Library is the canonical list of the user's Automations. It supports search, sort/filter, enabled/disabled state, owner/scope, last run, next trigger when determinable, current active revision, connection/permission health and create/duplicate/share/delete/recover operations.
Home dashboard cards MUST open the canonical Automation or AutomationRun rather than creating separate dashboard state. The landing page SHOULD make Create Automation prominent without forcing a user into an empty graph before they understand what they are creating.
Canonical entities
Automation MUST have stable AutomationID, Name, Description?, Icon?, Owner/Scope, Enabled/OperationalState, GraphID, DraftRevisionID, ActiveRevisionID?, InputSchema?, OutputSchema?, TriggerSummary, RequiredCapabilities, ExecutionPolicy, CreatedAt, ModifiedAt and Revision.
AutomationRun MUST have stable RunID, AutomationID, pinned AutomationRevisionID, TriggerID/TriggerEventID, Status, StartedAt, FinishedAt?, typed Inputs, typed Outputs?, NodeExecutionStates, Error?, approval/wait state, causal ancestry and audit/ActionGraph references.
Editing, renaming, moving, sharing or changing the landing-page position of an Automation MUST NOT change AutomationID. A Run is historical execution state and MUST remain bound to the exact Automation revision it executed.
Draft and Active revisions
Automations use the Node Graph Framework's Draft/Active revision model. Editing an active Automation changes a Draft revision. New trigger executions continue using the current Active revision until the user validates and activates/publishes a newer Draft.
An already-running Run remains pinned to its starting revision even if another revision is activated. Activation is atomic. Previous valid Active revisions remain available for inspection and rollback subject to retention policy.
Graph editor and simple creation
The graph is the canonical executable definition. Automations MAY offer simple When / If / Then creation, templates or natural-language creation, but these are graph-authoring views over the same GraphID rather than separate simplified formats. Opening an Automation MUST always allow inspection of the real graph.
The primary advanced editor uses the Home-owned Node Graph Framework with Automations' capability profile, typed ports, pan/zoom, selection, grouping/comments, copy/paste, undo/redo, validation, Draft/Active state and execution overlays.
Node search and connector interaction
Node creation/search MUST follow an Unreal-style graph interaction pattern. Right-clicking empty graph space opens the node list at that location; the user can immediately type to filter/search registered node types and select a result to create the node at/near the invocation point. Results SHOULD be grouped by meaningful categories while search ranks direct action/event/type matches first.
Connector deletion MUST support Ctrl-click directly on a connection/connector to remove it. Right-clicking a connection opens its context menu with Delete Connector as an explicit action. Keyboard-accessible selection plus Delete/Backspace MUST provide an equivalent non-pointer path. Deleting a connector removes only that connection, never either connected node.
Search results come from the live registered node catalogue for the current capability profile, target platform/device availability and installed/connected integrations. Automations MUST NOT maintain a stale hard-coded copy of the ecosystem's available actions.
Trigger model
Minimum trigger families:
* Manual — explicit user/API invocation.
* Schedule — timezone-aware one-time or repeating schedules such as a specific time, daily/weekly rules or interval schedules.
* App Event — typed events published by 9to1 apps.
* Condition/Watch — reevaluate a typed predicate when relevant state changes or on an explicitly declared evaluation cadence where event-driven evaluation is unavailable.
* External/Connector Event — supported webhooks/provider events/plugin/MCP/connector events.
* Automation invocation — typed call from another Automation.
Triggers use typed payloads. Schedule triggers preserve timezone/DST semantics. Event-driven state change MUST be preferred to wasteful polling when an owning capability provides an event/change feed. Trigger delivery MUST have stable identity/deduplication semantics.
Node families
The Automations capability profile MUST include registered node families needed for mature workflow composition, including:
* Triggers.
* 9to1 app Actions and Queries.
* Device Actions.
* Third-party app/service Actions.
* Conditions, Switch/branch and comparisons.
* Variables, constants, data access and transforms/conversions.
* Wait/Delay.
* For Each/iteration.
* Parallel/Fan-out and Join.
* Approval/Human review.
* Retry, On Failure, fallback and error handling.
* Call Automation.
* Dulche/Agent/Skill/Plugin/MCP/Connector capabilities.
* Typed Output/Return.
Connections are type-checked through the Node Graph Framework. Incompatible ports cannot connect unless a registered explicit conversion/transform exists.
Device-level actions
Automations MUST expose an extensive device-level action catalogue sourced directly from the capabilities actually advertised by the current/selected Home or Mesh device. Device actions are not a small hand-maintained Automations list. When a device/runtime exposes a supported typed action, Automations can surface it subject to OS/device permissions and the Home trust broker.
Representative device actions include, where the device advertises them:
* Wi-Fi on/off and supported network-selection/state operations.
* Bluetooth on/off and supported connection/device operations.
* Always On Display on/off plus supported AOD profiles/settings.
* Lock Screen Clock position, design/style and other supported lock-screen clock properties.
* Display/brightness, sound/volume, notification/DND, power/battery, input, connectivity and other device settings/actions exposed safely by the device capability registry.
Every device action node records the required DeviceID/capability/action version or an explicit compatible-device targeting policy. The editor MUST warn when an action is device-specific or not portable and explain that it may not work on another device. Validation on another device MUST report capability mismatch rather than silently substituting a different action.
Cross-device execution uses Mesh typed remote capability invocation and therefore passes both caller-side and target-device permission/policy checks. Automations MUST NOT turn device actions into a generic remote-desktop or arbitrary-code-execution channel.
Third-party app and service actions
Automations MUST surface typed third-party app/service actions wherever an installed app, plugin, connector, MCP capability, operating-system integration or registered provider exposes them. Discovery is dynamic and versioned, not a fixed list baked into Automations.
Third-party actions carry the originating capability/provider identity, connection/account requirements, input/output schemas, platform/device availability and risk/side-effect classification. Missing/uninstalled apps or expired connections place affected nodes into a clear Needs Attention/capability-unavailable state.
Example: a Schedule trigger at 16:00 may connect to a registered YouTube/compatible media action that plays a specified video on a selected compatible device. The workflow remains a typed trigger-to-action graph; Automations does not emulate YouTube by screen clicking.
Natural-language graph creation and editing
Dulche can create and modify Automations from natural-language requests, but the result MUST be a real editable Node Graph mutation using typed Node Graph APIs. Generated natural-language descriptions are explanatory only and are never the canonical workflow definition.
AI-generated graphs MUST validate node/action schemas, connection types, permissions/capabilities and target availability before activation. The editor SHOULD visually highlight nodes/connections added or changed by the most recent AI operation and allow ordinary undo.
Data, variables and nullability
Each Run has a typed data environment. Trigger payload fields, node outputs, variables and action inputs can be connected directly where types are compatible. Data transforms use explicit registered nodes/functions rather than implicit lossy conversion.
False, null, unavailable/redacted and error are distinct. Missing data MUST NOT silently become zero, False or an empty string and accidentally take the wrong branch.
Durable Wait and resume
Wait/Delay MUST be durable. A Run that waits for seconds, days, a time/date, device availability, approval or another supported condition persists a continuation record and releases active execution resources. It MUST NOT depend on an application thread/process literally sleeping.
Restart/redeployment must resume a valid waiting Run from persisted state without repeating already-committed side effects. ResumeAt/condition metadata and revision identity are inspectable.
Approval nodes
Approval/Human Review is a first-class node. It pauses a Run with WaitingForApproval and presents the intended decision/action to the appropriate authorised user. Approval, rejection, timeout and cancellation are explicit outcomes usable by subsequent graph branches.
An Approval node is distinct from Home's permission broker. Approval expresses workflow-required human review; the broker determines whether the caller is authorised to execute the protected action. Either mechanism may independently block execution.
Permissions, connections and secret handling
Each Automation has a stable caller identity bound to AutomationID/workspace identity. Activating a revision MUST show/derive the capabilities and action scopes the active graph requires. Expanding an Automation from a lower-risk action such as Mail.CreateDraft to Mail.Send or adding a new device/provider scope requires normal permission/trust reevaluation.
Secrets, tokens and provider credentials MUST NOT be stored as plaintext node properties. Nodes reference Home/connector-managed ConnectionID/secret handles. Sharing a graph does not automatically share the owner's credentials, external account access or trust grants.
Execution location and device targeting
Execution policy MUST make where the workflow can run explicit. Supported executors may include 9to1 cloud, the current Home/device runtime, a selected compatible Mesh device or a provider-native executor where that provider/action supports it.
The UI MUST NOT claim that a device-bound Automation will execute while all required devices are offline. Conversely, a cloud-capable workflow MUST NOT unnecessarily depend on an open desktop UI.
A device-targetable node may require a specific DeviceID, any compatible paired device or the triggering device according to its declared targeting policy. If no compatible device is available, the Run follows its configured wait/retry/failure policy with an explicit DeviceCapabilityUnavailable/DeviceOffline state.
Run lifecycle and operational state
Automation definition operational states include at least Draft, Enabled, Disabled and NeedsAttention. AutomationRun states include at least Queued, Running, Waiting, WaitingForApproval, Paused, Completed, Failed and Cancelled.
Disabling an Automation prevents new trigger starts but does not silently delete history. If Runs are already active, the UI must explicitly offer a policy such as allow existing Runs to finish, pause them where safe, or cancel them.
Home dashboard/Library status MUST be derived from canonical definition/run/connection state, not a separately editable status field.
Run history and execution inspection
Every Run has a structured execution timeline showing trigger, node start/end, typed input/output summaries, target action, attempt number, duration, waiting/approval state, result/error and causal child-run references. Sensitive values are redacted according to permissions.
The structured Run record is authoritative. Dulche may summarise it in natural language but MUST NOT invent events or hide failed/denied/cancelled nodes.
Users can open a historical Run against the exact pinned graph revision even after the current Automation has changed.
Error handling, retry and idempotency
An unhandled node failure stops the affected path by default. Authors may explicitly add retry, On Failure, fallback or continue semantics.
Retries of external or destructive actions MUST use the target action's idempotency/OperationID contract where available. If the runtime cannot determine whether a timed-out consequential action committed, it MUST enter a typed uncertain/Needs Attention state rather than blindly repeat an operation that could duplicate its external side effect.
Retry policies are bounded and inspectable; infinite automatic retry loops are prohibited.
Loop and cascade protection
Runs carry TriggerEventID, RunID, ParentRunID? and causal ancestry. The runtime MUST detect repeated event/run cycles, bound recursion/cascade depth and total execution budget, and deduplicate replayed trigger deliveries.
If an Automation repeatedly triggers itself or another Automation in a causal loop, the affected cascade is stopped with a diagnostic that identifies the loop rather than continuing to mutate user data indefinitely.
Calling other Automations
Call Automation invokes another Automation by stable AutomationID and declared InputSchema/OutputSchema; it does not copy the target graph into the caller. The callee keeps its own version, permissions and Run history while parent/child Run causality is linked.
Test, validate and run
The editor MUST distinguish Validate, Test and Run for real.
* Validate performs graph/schema/type/capability/permission/connection checks without executing actions.
* Test executes with selected sample/current data and MUST use action preview/dry-run facilities where the target capability provides them.
* Run for real executes the active or explicitly selected validated revision with normal side effects and permissions.
If a Test reaches an action that cannot be safely simulated, Automations must identify that limitation and require explicit real-execution confirmation before performing the side effect.
Sharing, teams and run-as identity
Automations MAY be shared within supported personal/team/workspace scopes. Sharing the definition does not transfer credentials, provider connections, device permissions or Always Trust grants.
Where shared execution supports multiple identities, run-as semantics MUST be explicit, such as triggering user versus Automation owner/service identity. The runtime MUST NOT silently choose whichever identity has greater authority.
Compatibility and migration
Every registered node type/action/event records schema/version identity. If an app/device/provider update retires or incompatibly changes a node schema, the graph enters NeedsAttention/migration state rather than silently dropping the node, retyping a port or changing behaviour.
Migration may be automatic only when semantics are provably equivalent; otherwise the editor must show the affected nodes and require review before reactivation.
Persistent contextual AI bar
Automations MUST host the global persistent Dulche AI bar. Its semantic context includes AutomationID, GraphID, Draft/Active revisions, selected NodeIDs/ConnectionIDs, validation state, Run/connection/permission state, registered node catalogue and typed graph mutation actions.
Read-only mode can explain/debug/inspect. Write mode may modify the graph only through typed Node Graph/Automation APIs. AI MUST NOT simulate graph mouse gestures.
Automations API
Automations' first-party API catalogue is exhaustive under the global API-parity rule. Minimum canonical entry points include:
9to1.Automations.List(filters?);
9to1.Automations.Get(automationID);
9to1.Automations.Create(config);
9to1.Automations.Update(automationID, patch);
9to1.Automations.Delete(automationID);
9to1.Automations.Restore(automationID);
9to1.Automations.Validate(automationID, revision?);
9to1.Automations.Activate(automationID, revision);
9to1.Automations.Disable(automationID);
9to1.Automations.Run(automationID, inputs?, revision?);
9to1.Automations.CancelRun(runID);
9to1.Automations.PauseRun(runID);
9to1.Automations.ResumeRun(runID);
9to1.Automations.GetRun(runID);
9to1.Automations.ListRuns(automationID, filters?);
9to1.Automations.RetryRun(runID, fromNodeID?);
9to1.Automations.ListAvailableActions(context?);
9to1.Automations.ListDeviceActions(deviceID?);
Graph editing remains on 9to1.NodeGraph.* rather than duplicating graph-mutation methods inside Automations. Every additional user-visible Automations operation — Library organisation, connection repair, permission review, execution-policy change, sharing, migration and run controls — requires equivalent typed API coverage.
Persistence and recovery
Automation definitions, Draft/Active revisions, Runs, wait/approval continuations, trigger cursors/deduplication state and connection references are durably versioned. A crash/restart MUST NOT restart the graph from the beginning and duplicate already-committed actions.
Normal Automation deletion is recoverable; permanent purge is explicit/high-risk. Run-history retention/purge follows declared policy and audit requirements.
Accessibility
The landing Home/Library, node graph and Run inspector MUST be keyboard-operable and accessible. Node search can be opened without a pointer; nodes, ports and connectors expose semantic labels/types; connection creation/deletion has keyboard equivalents; execution/error states cannot be conveyed by colour alone.
Graph zoom/pan must not be required to discover the textual meaning of a node. A structured accessible node/connection list or equivalent semantic representation MUST be available to assistive technology.
Performance and resource behaviour
Large graphs, Libraries and Run histories MUST virtualise where appropriate. Node catalogue search must remain responsive across extensive app/device/third-party action registries and should query/index incrementally rather than blocking on full capability rescans.
Execution is event-driven/durable; idle/waiting Runs must not retain unnecessary UI/execution threads. Run logs/timelines paginate/stream incrementally and caches are bounded.
Failure behaviour
Automations MUST return structured failures including AutomationNotFound, RunNotFound, InvalidGraph, ValidationFailed, NodeTypeUnavailable, ConnectionTypeMismatch, CapabilityUnavailable, DeviceCapabilityUnavailable, DeviceOffline, ProviderConnectionUnavailable, PermissionRequired, ApprovalRejected, ApprovalTimedOut, WaitResumeFailed, RevisionConflict, TriggerDuplicate, LoopDetected, ExecutionBudgetExceeded, UnsafeRetryState and MigrationRequired in addition to target-action errors.
A missing third-party app, disconnected provider or unavailable device never causes the runtime to pretend an action completed; affected definitions/runs surface Needs Attention or the configured wait/failure path.
Acceptance requirements
Automations is implementation-complete only when acceptance coverage verifies at least:
* Landing Home shows canonical operational dashboard state and Library lists persisted user Automations with search/filter/status/last-next-run information.
* Opening an Automation exposes its real Node Graph; simple/natural-language creation produces the same canonical graph rather than a hidden alternate workflow format.
* Right-click empty graph space opens an Unreal-style searchable node list; typing filters the live registered catalogue; Ctrl-click on a connector deletes it and right-click offers Delete Connector.
* Draft and Active revisions remain distinct; activating a new revision does not mutate an already-running Run pinned to an older revision.
* Manual, Schedule, App Event, Condition/Watch, external/provider and Automation-call triggers deliver typed payloads with deduplication identity.
* A representative extensive device action registry is discovered from real device capabilities, including available Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/AOD/lock-screen-clock actions, and device-specific portability warnings/capability validation are shown.
* Third-party app/service actions appear from installed/connected capability registries and missing/unavailable integrations enter a diagnosable Needs Attention state.
* A schedule at 16:00 can invoke a registered YouTube/compatible media Play action on a compatible target device without UI simulation.
* Natural-language graph creation/editing produces valid typed Node Graph mutations and remains fully inspectable/undoable.
* Durable Wait and Approval nodes survive process/device/runtime restart without replaying committed prior actions.
* Retries use idempotency semantics and uncertain external side effects do not blindly repeat.
* Self-triggering/cross-Automation loops are detected and stopped with causal diagnostics.
* Validate, Test and Run-for-real remain distinct and Test does not silently perform unsimulatable external actions.
* Shared Automations do not inherit another user's credentials/device permissions/trust grants and run-as identity remains explicit.
* Schema/version changes place incompatible graphs into migration/Needs Attention rather than silently altering behaviour.
* The persistent AI bar inspects/edits graphs only through semantic context and typed APIs.
* Large node catalogues/graphs/run histories remain responsive through indexing, virtualisation and incremental loading.
* When Home is absent at process start, Automations follows the global Install Home/bootstrap contract rather than launching an incompatible private permission/runtime stack.

Dev
Product role and engineering principle
9-1 Dev is the native CUI professional software-development environment. It MUST be fully useful without AI and provide mature project/workspace management, source editing, language tooling, build/run/test, debugging, terminal access, package/dependency management, source-control integration, visual CUI development, extension development, remote/container environments and structured agentic coding.
Dev is the authoritative code-development surface. Specialised products such as Stack, Sites and AI Studio retain their own domain authority, but Dev can open, inspect, edit and run their developer-facing project resources through stable shared identities and typed APIs.
Repository-aware AI mutations MUST use typed code/file/project/task actions and MUST expose the resulting reviewable change set. Opaque desktop automation MUST NOT be used when a structured development action exists.
Canonical workspace and project model
DevWorkspace has stable WorkspaceID, Roots[], Projects[], OpenEditors[], Tasks[], RunConfigurations[], DebugConfigurations[], Toolchains[], Environments[], SourceControlBindings[], ExtensionState, WorkspaceSettings, CreatedAt, ModifiedAt and Revision.
A workspace may contain multiple folders, repositories and related projects. Monorepos, client/server solutions and multi-language workspaces MUST NOT require flattening into one artificial project type.
Project has stable ProjectID, ProjectTypeID, language/framework metadata, source roots, build system, package/dependency metadata, target platforms, toolchain requirements, run/debug configurations, preview providers and Revision. Dev SHOULD consume existing ecosystem project files rather than replacing them with a proprietary project model where an established project format exists.
New Project workflow and project catalogue
File → New Project opens a searchable/filterable catalogue analogous to mature IDE project creation. Filters include language, framework, platform, project type, target runtime, installed toolchains, 9to1 product/surface and organisation templates.
First-party examples include console applications, CUI applications, class/static/shared libraries, web/API services, test projects, Python packages/CLI applications, Sites projects, Android/mobile projects, operating-system/kernel/bootloader projects, 9to1 extensions, CUI component libraries, AI provider/tool projects and other supported templates.
Project providers/extensions MAY register additional project templates, languages, frameworks and target types. The catalogue MUST NOT be hard-coded so tightly that adding a new ecosystem requires changing Dev core.
After selecting a project type Dev exposes only applicable framework/toolchain/runtime options and validates requirements before creation. Missing required SDK/toolchain components are shown explicitly with install/configure actions where supported.

source_text:
Editor and navigation
The source editor includes tabs, preview/pinned tabs, split editors, editor groups, breadcrumbs, outline/symbol view, optional minimap, line numbers, indentation/whitespace guides, bracket matching, folding, multi-cursor, rectangular selection, snippets, configurable keybindings, encoding/line-ending awareness, large-file mode and undo/redo.
Search/navigation includes file search, workspace text/regex search, go to line/file/symbol, references, implementations and structural/semantic search where the language provider supports it.
Editor state references canonical Files/project identity where possible rather than treating an absolute filesystem path as permanent identity.
Language intelligence and parsing
Dev uses established language tooling protocols/providers where practical. LSP or equivalent providers supply completion, hover, signature help, go-to-definition/declaration/type/implementation, references, rename, code actions, semantic diagnostics, document/workspace symbols, formatting and semantic tokens.
Tree-sitter or an equivalent maintained parser MAY provide fast syntax structure, incremental parsing, selections and editor features where suitable, while language-specific semantic operations remain owned by the relevant language/tooling provider.
Dev MUST NOT implement language semantics using fragile regex parsing where a maintained compiler/LSP/parser exists.
Toolchain Manager and built-in/provisionable toolchains
Dev provides a first-class Toolchain Manager. A Toolchain has stable ToolchainID, language, provider, compiler/runtime/interpreter, version, target architectures, debugger, language server, package manager, environment binding, capability state and provenance.
Core supported ecosystems SHOULD be usable out of the box through bundled or one-click provisionable toolchains where licensing/platform constraints permit. Examples include .NET SDK/Roslyn for C#/F#, LLVM/Clang for C/C++, CPython plus Python language/debug/package tooling, rustc/Cargo, a JDK for Java/Kotlin and the relevant JavaScript/TypeScript runtimes/tooling.
Python is treated correctly as a runtime/interpreter ecosystem rather than inaccurately labelling every execution as compilation. Native/package compilation tools may be added where project requirements need them.
Platform-native toolchains such as MSVC may be discovered and used when installed. Remote/container environments expose their own toolchains through the same abstraction.
Missing compiler/runtime indication
Dev MUST make toolchain readiness obvious before build/run. It must distinguish missing compiler/runtime, wrong version, missing debugger, missing language server, missing package manager, registry/authentication failure and general build failure.
A project requirement such as '.NET SDK >= 10', 'clang >= 20' or 'Python 3.14' is compared against the selected environment. The UI shows Ready or explicit environment issues with required versus installed versions.
Errors such as command-not-found or process spawn failure MUST NOT be the primary user experience when Dev can determine that a required toolchain component is missing. Supported components can be installed/configured directly through a typed toolchain operation.
Build pipeline and tasks
Dev supports structured Tasks and BuildPipelines. A pipeline may contain Restore, Generate, Compile, Link, Package, Test, Sign or other project-defined stages with dependencies, parallelism rules, environment, working directory, cancellation, timeout and diagnostics matching.
Build UI exposes stage-level state such as pending/running/succeeded/failed/cancelled and routes compiler/linter/build diagnostics into the common Problems model.
Tasks can be project-defined, extension-provided or inferred from recognised ecosystem files, but generated/inferred tasks remain inspectable and editable.
Run configurations and target-aware Run
Run means execute the selected project's declared launch target rather than universally starting one host executable. RunConfiguration has stable ID, provider/type, target artifact/project, arguments, environment, working directory, target platform/device, pre-launch tasks, preview provider and Revision.
Examples include console → terminal, web → development server + preview, Android → emulator/device install + launch, CUI application → application runtime, 9to1 extension → extension development host, operating system → virtual machine, and library → test/sample host where configured.
The Run selector shows the exact active target and environment. Dev MUST NOT silently run a different configuration because another panel gained focus.
