Debugger
Dev provides a full debugger using DAP or another maintained abstraction where practical. Supported capabilities include launch/attach, source/conditional breakpoints, hit-count breakpoints where supported, logpoints, continue/pause, step into/over/out, call stack, scopes, variables, watches, expression evaluation, threads/processes and exception breakpoints.
Capabilities are negotiated per debugger/provider; Dev MUST NOT expose controls that imply unsupported debugger semantics.
Testing and Test Explorer
Testing is a first-class typed subsystem. Test Explorer shows project/suite/test identity, running/passed/failed/skipped state, duration, failure output, source location and rerun capability.
Users and AI can run one test, a selection, file/suite/project/workspace set or previously failed tests. Test results have stable identities and are available to AI/change review without scraping terminal output.
Problems and diagnostics
Compiler, language-server, linter, build, package and test failures feed a common Problems model. Diagnostic records include provider/source, severity, message, code, file/resource identity, range and related information/quick fixes where available.
Diagnostics are semantic Dev objects consumable by UI, APIs and Dulche; they are not only coloured text in a terminal.
Terminal integration
Dev uses the shared Terminal runtime rather than implementing an incompatible second terminal emulator. It supports multiple tabs/panes, shell profiles, project/environment working-directory binding, environment variables, command history, task integration and clickable file/line diagnostics where supported.
A Dev terminal remains a real shell terminal and does not require AI for ordinary command execution. Terminal actions use shared Terminal APIs when canonical.
Source control and Stack integration
Stack remains the canonical 9to1 source-control/collaboration product. Dev presents working-tree/project source-control state and uses Stack/Git APIs for changed files, hunks, staged/unstaged state where applicable, branch/twig/leaf state, history, blame, conflicts, upstream state and other supported collaboration context.
Dev MUST NOT implement a separate competing project/branch model that diverges from Stack. It can expose conventional Git concepts directly when the backing repository uses them and map Stack-specific structures through the Stack contract.
Source-control state is accessible without AI and is also available to Dulche/agents as typed context.
Diff and review editor
Dev provides side-by-side, unified/inline and word-level diff views with file navigation, hunk/line selection where safe, staging/reverting, conflict resolution and navigation between changes.
Diff targets include working tree versus source-control base, branch/Stack comparisons, commits and AI change sets. Each comparison MUST identify its left/right revisions explicitly.
AI-generated changes MUST NOT bypass normal diff/review visibility.
AI ChangeSet model
Every mutating AI coding pass has a stable AIChangeSetID recording initiating task/prompt, model/agent identity where available, starting workspace/repository revision, exact file operations/patches, created/deleted/moved resources, child-agent contributions, tests/tasks run, diagnostics before/after, completion status and timestamps.
Dev distinguishes the AI-pass diff from the overall working-tree diff. Existing user modifications are not relabelled as AI-authored merely because an AI later edited the same file.
Revert AI Change attempts to reverse only the recorded AI patch/change set while preserving unrelated user changes. If later overlapping edits prevent safe automatic reversal, Dev surfaces a conflict rather than discarding work.
AI review workflow
Dev supports Review first and Apply then review workflows. Review first presents proposed patches before application; Apply then review applies scoped edits and immediately exposes them in the AI review surface. Workspace/user policy selects the default.
Review supports accept/reject by file and hunk, and finer region/line review where the patch model can apply it safely. AI may attach explanatory review annotations to hunks without inserting those explanations as source comments.
Review summaries include build/test/diagnostic outcomes where they were actually run, for example build passed, tests passed/failed, new warnings and resolved diagnostics. Dev MUST NOT claim tests/builds succeeded unless those executions occurred.
Structured AI coding and agentic development
Dulche/agent context includes workspace/project/repository identity, selected files/ranges/symbols, diagnostics, references/call relationships where available, tests, tasks/builds, source-control state, package state, terminal/run results and relevant preview state.
AI actions use typed operations such as read/search file, find symbol/references, create/move/delete file, apply patch/edit, semantic refactor, run task/test, inspect diagnostics, inspect diff, manage approved package operations and invoke owning shared APIs.
Longer agentic development can inspect, plan, edit, build/test, diagnose, iterate and present the final change set within an explicit scope. Agent Activity exposes current goal, operation, files examined/changed, validation, blockers, retries, subtasks/child agents and pending human decisions.
Parallel agents require scoped workspaces/branches/worktrees or another safe isolation/reconciliation mechanism. They MUST NOT blindly race edits against the same canonical files.
Symbol-aware editing and refactoring
Dev exposes code symbols such as class/type, function/method, property/field, interface, namespace/module and references when supplied by the language provider. AI and manual operations SHOULD target semantic symbols where possible rather than fragile character offsets.
Refactoring uses language/provider semantics where available: rename symbol, extract method/function, inline, move symbol, organise imports, change signature, safe delete and generate/implement members. Global text replacement MUST NOT substitute for a supported semantic refactor.

source_text:
Dependency integrity and reproducibility
Dev respects ecosystem lockfiles and project-local version constraints. Package operations SHOULD be reproducible and show manifest/lockfile diffs.
When authoritative advisory metadata is available Dev may surface known vulnerabilities, deprecated/yanked versions, licence metadata and conflicts. It MUST distinguish an external advisory from an AI-generated suspicion.
Offline/network/authentication states are represented accurately rather than collapsing every package restore problem into a generic build failure.
Native 9to1 extension platform
Dev is the primary development/debugging environment for a shared native 9to1 Extension platform. Extensions MAY contribute language/toolchain/debugger/formatter/linter providers, project templates, package providers, editors, commands, tool windows, CUI/visual-builder components, AI context/tools, Node Graph node types and product-specific contributions exposed by host APIs.
One extension package may target multiple 9to1 products through explicit contribution contracts; products do not need separate unrelated plugin formats for the same extension.
Extensions use a versioned manifest declaring ExtensionID, publisher/name/version, compatible host/API versions, entry points, target products, contributions, permissions/capabilities, dependencies, supported platforms, assets, update channel and signature/provenance.
Extension permissions, isolation and trust
Extensions declare required capabilities such as workspace read/write, process execution, network, terminal, credential access, Files, Stack or AI/model access. The host can present permissions during install/enable; low-risk themes/components MUST NOT silently inherit arbitrary process/filesystem/network rights.
Extension execution is isolated where practical with crash containment, startup timeout, resource monitoring, per-extension logs, disable/restart and safe-mode recovery. A broken extension SHOULD NOT crash-loop the whole Dev process.
Extension APIs are versioned/capability-negotiated. Deprecated APIs produce migration diagnostics and compatibility behaviour where reasonable rather than silent breakage.
Extension development host and inspector
Run on a 9to1 Extension project can launch the selected target product's clean Extension Host with the development extension loaded and debugger/logging attached. Multi-target extensions offer explicit target-host run choices.
Extension Inspector exposes registered contributions, activated services, requested permissions, host/API compatibility, logs/errors, extension-host state and performance/resource information where available.
Extension integration tests can target selected hosts and permissions without requiring installation into the developer's normal production profile.

source_text:
Visual CUI Builder
Dev MUST include a native visual CUI builder for CUI applications/components. The core layout is Component Tree + Visual Canvas + contextual Inspector, with source editing available alongside it.
The builder exposes registered CUI controls/components such as text, buttons, inputs, switches, selectors, menus, tabs, lists/tables/trees, cards/panels, dialogs, navigation, images/media, canvas/chart surfaces and project-defined components.
Visual editing manipulates the same canonical CUI representation/source model used by the runtime. Dev MUST NOT maintain a hidden proprietary canvas model that drifts from or overwrites hand-written CUI source.
Visual CUI layout, properties and bindings
The CUI builder supports hierarchy/nesting, reorder, grid/flex/dock-style layout according to CUI's real layout model, padding/margin/gap, alignment, min/max sizing, responsive behaviour, breakpoints, visibility/overflow and other supported CUI layout properties.
The Inspector exposes real component properties grouped into content, layout, appearance, behaviour/events, data bindings and accessibility. Editing an Inspector property changes the canonical source/model and source changes update the canvas.
Bindings such as model property → UI property and command/event bindings are first-class typed objects where CUI supports them. Simple event-handler creation can generate/navigate to real source handlers; graph-based behaviour may use the shared Node Graph Framework where the project architecture chooses it.
CUI states, component authoring and accessibility
Visual preview supports representative states such as default, hover, pressed, focused, disabled, selected, loading, empty and validation error where components expose them.
Developers can visually author reusable custom CUI components with typed properties/events/slots and reuse them throughout a project.
The builder continuously surfaces accessibility diagnostics such as missing labels, contrast problems, focus-order issues, unreachable controls, inadequate target size and colour-only state. These diagnostics integrate with the normal Problems model.
Two-way source and visual round-trip
Selecting a component in source/tree SHOULD highlight it in the visual preview where source mapping exists; selecting/inspecting a rendered element SHOULD reveal the owning component/source symbol/range where safe.
Hand-written/custom constructs that cannot be represented by a visual editor remain code-defined and preserved. The builder MUST NOT delete or rewrite unsupported code merely to force visual round-tripping.
Visual AI edits such as 'make this sidebar collapse below 800px' mutate real CUI properties/layout/source through typed actions and therefore appear in normal code/AI diffs.
Live split view and preview providers
Dev supports flexible split layouts including Code | Preview, Code | Diff, Diff | Preview, Code | Terminal, Code | Tests, Code | AI and debugger-oriented layouts. Workspace/project layouts can be saved.
PreviewProvider is a typed project/extension capability. Representative providers include CUI live render, Sites/web preview, Markdown render, extension host/sample host, AI Studio tool test harness, Android emulator/device and OS virtual-machine display/serial view.
In Code | Preview mode, the developer can resize/swap panes and optionally Follow editor or Pin a particular component/page/application preview while editing related files.
Hot reload and last-valid preview
Where the selected runtime supports it, source changes trigger incremental build/hot reload into the preview. Preview state clearly distinguishes Live, Building, Reloading, Build failed, Disconnected and Paused.
If a new build fails, Dev preserves the last valid preview when technically possible and overlays/links the new diagnostics rather than replacing useful state with a blank pane.
PreviewConfiguration can retain viewport/device, route/component target, theme/state/sample data, environment and other provider-specific design-time inputs.
Interactive preview and source inspection
Applicable previews are interactive. CUI/web previews can accept pointer/keyboard/navigation input, resize, hover/focus state and other runtime interactions without becoming the general Browse product.
Inspect element can expose component/type, source file/range, runtime bounds, computed style/layout, bindings, accessibility state and event handlers where the preview provider supplies mappings.
Responsive preview presets include phone, tablet, desktop and custom sizes where applicable.
Visual diff and AI preview validation
UI-oriented change review MAY offer Code diff | Visual diff and/or Diff | Preview. Source diff remains authoritative; visual comparison supplements engineering review rather than replacing it.
Where a preview provider supports before/after rendering, AI review can show previous/current render or affected component state and link visual differences back to the associated source changes.
AI-generated UI work SHOULD perform build/runtime/visual validation when the required preview/inspection capability is available and within scope. Passing compilation alone is not sufficient evidence that a visual task is correct.
Remote, container and reproducible environments
Dev supports environment adapters such as Local, WSL where available, SSH remote, devcontainer/container, cloud development environment and other extension-provided environments.
File operations, LSP/toolchains, tasks, debugging and package operations execute in the selected environment where appropriate. Remote development SHOULD run language servers/build tools near the project filesystem rather than blindly copying whole repositories to the client.
Dev recognises project-native environment definitions such as devcontainer.json rather than replacing them with an incompatible format.
Workspace trust and execution security
Opening a repository does not automatically trust or execute repository-controlled code. Workspace Trust controls execution of tasks/build scripts, package lifecycle scripts, debugger launch, extension recommendations, VM boot/run configurations and other code-execution surfaces.
Dev clearly separates reading/editing files from launching code, installing packages, network access, credential access, privilege elevation and deployment/external side effects.
Secrets/tokens use shared credential infrastructure where possible and MUST NOT be unnecessarily exposed to AI context, logs, source control, telemetry or generated diffs.

source_text:
Browse
9to1 Browse is a full Firefox-derived browser product with native CUI chrome and native CUI internal surfaces. Firefox/Gecko is the primary donor, default web engine and behavioural baseline. Chromium/Blink is a first-class secondary browser/rendering backend available per tab. Browse MUST remain one coherent browser with one canonical 9to1-owned tab/session model; Chromium support MUST NOT be implemented as a second browser bolted onto Firefox or as a separate user profile universe.
Donor authority and parity
Firefox donor parity is the minimum supported capability set, not the finished feature ceiling. Unless a feature is explicitly replaced, excluded or made incompatible by an approved 9to1 architecture decision, Browse MUST retain mature Firefox functionality and quality-of-life behaviour.
* Tabs and windows, including restore/reopen behaviour, pinned tabs and normal navigation history.
* Profiles, bookmarks, history, downloads, browsing-data controls, site permissions, privacy/security controls and appropriate password/passkey integration.
* Firefox developer tooling, reader/media functionality, picture-in-picture where donor-supported, accessibility, keyboard navigation, crash/session recovery and mature settings/configuration.
* WebExtension compatibility to the maximum extent supported by the retained Firefox APIs, with unsupported or engine-specific APIs surfaced explicitly rather than silently ignored.
All Firefox proprietary or embedded AI surfaces are non-authoritative and MUST be removed or replaced by Dulche-backed 9to1 surfaces. The agent MUST NOT preserve a Firefox AI sidebar, chatbot, assistant or proprietary AI integration merely for donor parity.
Web engine architecture
Each web BrowserTab selects a WebEngine value of Firefox/Gecko or Chromium/Blink. The normal user-facing choice SHOULD be labelled Firefox and Chromium; implementation and diagnostics MAY additionally expose the underlying Gecko and Blink engine names. Gecko is the default unless the user or a persisted site rule selects Chromium.
Changing a tab between Firefox and Chromium changes the renderer/backend used for the page, not the canonical identity of the tab, workspace or Browse session. Switching engines reloads/reconstructs the document through the selected backend. Engine-private runtime state such as DOM objects, JavaScript heaps and renderer-process memory is not required to transfer.
Browse MUST own canonical higher-level browser entities instead of allowing Gecko and Chromium to directly share raw profile databases. At minimum the architecture must model BrowserProfile, BrowserTab, NavigationEntry, Bookmark, HistoryEntry, Download, SitePermission, Workspace, TabGroup, SplitView, SearchProvider, SiteEnhancer and EnginePreference as typed 9to1-owned entities or equivalent strongly typed contracts.
Gecko and Chromium MUST be isolated internally. They MUST NOT be pointed at the same physical cookie/profile/session database. Engine adapters translate the relevant canonical Browse state into each backend and propagate supported changes back to Browse.
Users MUST be able to use Firefox for this tab, Chromium for this tab, always Firefox for a site/domain, always Chromium for a site/domain, and reset a persisted site engine preference. A broken page SHOULD be switchable to the other engine with one obvious action without opening a separate browser product.
Automatic upstream maintenance
The Firefox/Gecko and Chromium/Blink frameworks MUST be maintained continuously against the latest appropriate upstream release and MUST automatically detect and ingest newer upstream versions when available. A long-lived stale engine is a maintenance defect.
Automatic update does not mean blindly shipping an unvalidated upstream binary. The update pipeline MUST fetch/rebase or reapply maintained 9to1 changes, build the affected engine integration, run Browse compatibility and regression suites, verify CUI integration, engine switching, extension baselines, session/profile isolation, Site Enhancer behaviour, DevTools integration and Dulche browser capabilities, and promote the new engine only after the applicable acceptance gates pass. Security-sensitive upstream releases receive expedited priority. The previous known-good engine build MUST remain rollback-capable until promotion is proven stable.
CUI and URI namespace contract
Browse has four distinct first-class content namespaces. They MUST remain architecturally and security-distinct even when multiple namespaces ultimately render through CUI.
* cui:// — generic CUI-rendered surfaces and extension-defined/custom CUI pages. This is the general CUI namespace and is not synonymous with Browse internals.
* browse:// — Browse-owned internal pages such as browse://newtab, browse://settings, browse://downloads, browse://history, browse://extensions and other Browse-owned management surfaces.
* 9to1:// — native 9to1 application surfaces hosted inside a Browse tab, for example 9to1://Spaces, 9to1://Write or a typed deep link such as 9to1://Write/<resource>. These are the actual application surfaces, not web versions or reduced browser copies.
* https:// and http:// — ordinary web content. User-facing normal web navigation uses these web schemes; Browse-owned, CUI and native-app content MUST NOT masquerade as an HTTP(S) origin.
Internal compatibility plumbing inherited from donors MAY exist only where technically unavoidable, but it MUST NOT be exposed as a competing public routing model. The 9to1 routing contract above is authoritative.
Native 9to1 app surfaces in tabs
Opening 9to1://<App> MUST instantiate the real CUI application surface and the real application services inside the Browse tab. It MUST NOT load a separately implemented web edition, feature-reduced embedded edition or imitation of the app. Responsive layout adaptation is allowed and expected; capability divergence merely because the app is hosted in Browse is not.
9to1:// routes MUST be registered centrally by the application/router registry and support typed deep links to canonical resources where the owning app supports them. A tab title and icon should reflect the actual resource/app instead of exposing an opaque route string as its primary label.
The same canonical app data/state MUST be addressed regardless of whether the app is opened in its normal standalone surface or through 9to1:// in Browse. Opening the same Write document, Board, Space or Data workbook in multiple valid surfaces MUST NOT silently create disconnected copies.
9to1 native app tabs participate in normal Browse capabilities including tab groups, pinning, workspaces, restore/reopen and Split View. A user can therefore place 9to1://Write with a research document beside an https:// research page, or combine two different native 9to1 apps, without requiring a separate web version of either app.
Profiles and workspaces
Browser profiles are tab-scoped, not window-scoped. Every BrowserTab carries a ProfileID or equivalent profile context, allowing one window, one workspace and one Split View to contain tabs from different profiles simultaneously.
A BrowserProfile is an identity/storage/privacy boundary. Depending on supported configuration, it owns or scopes cookies, login sessions, site storage, site permissions, browsing-data attribution, extensions and extension state, search preferences, Site Enhancers, credentials/passkeys and other profile-specific browser configuration.
A Workspace is an organisational/session construct rather than an identity boundary. A workspace may contain tabs from multiple profiles and owns organisational state such as open tabs, groups, split arrangements, workspace pins and layout. Switching workspace MUST NOT inherently sign the user into or out of websites.
Profile identity MUST be visually discoverable on tabs and in relevant browser UI so the user can tell which account/session context will be used. Consequential actions and Dulche-controlled actions SHOULD make the active profile context clear where confusion could cause the action to occur under the wrong identity.
Changing a tab to another profile MUST reopen/recreate its web session under the destination profile rather than copying authentication material across profile boundaries. Safe navigation/organisation metadata such as URL, group, workspace and split position may be preserved where applicable.
Tabs, groups and placement
Browse MUST provide modern tab management in addition to Firefox donor parity. Tab groups are first-class canonical entities with stable identity, naming, optional colour/icon metadata, collapse/expand state, persistence, restore, drag/drop and movement between windows/workspaces. Dulche and other typed APIs can address a group directly.
Tab-strip placement MUST be a first-class configurable preference with full feature parity in all four orientations:
* Horizontal tabs at the top.
* Horizontal tabs at the bottom.
* Vertical tabs on the left.
* Vertical tabs on the right.
The interface MUST adapt properly to each orientation rather than mechanically moving a top strip. Groups, pinned tabs, profile indicators, drag/reorder, tab search, previews, context menus, engine state where surfaced, close/reopen, Dulche mentions and split operations MUST remain functional in every orientation. Compact/collapsed and appropriate auto-expand behaviours may be provided as configurable presentation options.
Split View
Split View displays two independent BrowserTab entities side-by-side in one browser content area with a resizable divider. The split container owns presentation only; each pane remains a real tab with its own URL/route, navigation history, profile, renderer/backend where applicable and canonical tab identity.
A split may mix any compatible tab surface classes, including web + web, 9to1 app + web, 9to1 app + 9to1 app, Browse internal + web and tabs from different BrowserProfiles. Either pane can be swapped, unsplit or moved without destroying the underlying tab.
The two-pane experience is the required baseline. The architecture SHOULD avoid assumptions that make future multi-pane layouts impossible, but more than two panes is not required unless separately specified.

source_text:
Search and AI entry
The primary New Tab/address search entry MUST expose two explicit modes: Search and AI. Search is the default. The active mode is clearly visible and switchable quickly, including by keyboard.
Search mode performs normal navigation/search behaviour and MUST NOT invoke an LLM merely to execute an ordinary URL or provider query. AI mode sends the request to Dulche and can use permissioned Browse capabilities and referenced browser/app context.
Browse MUST support a typed SearchProvider contract and allow the user to configure a default provider plus an optional secondary provider. Providers may supply query construction, suggestions and declared privacy/capability metadata. Extension-defined providers may participate through the same contract.
Browse MUST support searching two providers at once. Dual-provider search creates one real tab per provider for the same query and places those tabs into the standard Split View, one provider per pane. This MUST reuse normal BrowserTab and SplitView infrastructure rather than a bespoke dual-search renderer. Single-provider search remains the normal default unless the user configures otherwise.
Dulche browser experience
Dulche is the only authoritative AI system in Browse. Firefox-provided proprietary AI surfaces MUST be removed/replaced. Browse SHOULD provide both a persistent Dulche sidebar for larger tasks and a lightweight floating/command bar for contextual requests, using the shared Dulche runtime rather than launching a browser-specific model server.
The Dulche UI MUST support @-mentioning canonical browser context. At minimum users can mention tabs and SHOULD be able to mention tab groups, workspaces, split panes and other supported Browse entities. Mention autocomplete resolves to stable canonical IDs rather than copying only titles/URLs into the prompt.
Examples include comparing @Durham with @York, summarising all tabs in @Coursework, or asking Dulche to use a referenced 9to1://Write document together with an https:// research tab. Where the referenced surface is a native 9to1 app, Dulche MUST use that app's semantic APIs rather than screen-scraping its CUI.
Permissioned autonomous browsing
With explicit user permission, Dulche can autonomously operate Browse for a task. A request such as 'scroll through YouTube and pick out some good videos' may inspect visible/accessible results, scroll, open candidates, compare them and return recommendations without requiring confirmation for every benign intermediate interaction.
Permission scope MUST be explicit and composable. The implementation must support equivalents of read this page, control this tab, control these selected tabs and control Browse for this task. Granting one scope MUST NOT silently grant permanent global browser control.
Browser automation SHOULD use structured semantic capabilities such as Navigate, OpenTab, CloseTab, ActivateTab, ReadPage, ReadElement, Find, Scroll, Click, FillField, SelectOption, GoBack, GoForward and Reload when structured control exists. Blind coordinate input is a fallback, not the primary architecture.
Consequential external actions remain governed by the shared 9to1 permission/confirmation policy. Purchases, publishing/sending, destructive account changes, security changes, credential disclosure/entry and comparable external side effects MUST NOT become implicitly authorised merely because Dulche was permitted to browse.
Extensions and CUI extension surfaces
Firefox/WebExtension compatibility MUST be retained to the maximum practical extent. Because a tab may use Firefox/Gecko or Chromium/Blink, extension capability MUST be explicit. An extension may be Gecko-compatible, Chromium-compatible through supported adapters, compatible with both, Browse/CUI-only, partially compatible or unsupported in the active engine.
Switching one tab to Chromium MUST NOT silently uninstall an extension, disable it globally or make it disappear. Engine-specific limitations MUST be surfaced predictably.
Extensions can register supported CUI surfaces using cui:// routing and the extension CUI API, including settings pages, dashboards, sidebars, tool panels, New Tab components or other permitted custom pages. CUI rendering permission does not imply unrestricted Browse or 9to1 internal access; capabilities remain sandboxed and permission-scoped.

source_text:
Files, drag/drop and cross-app integration
Browse retains a mature Download entity/lifecycle while completed files integrate with the shared Files system so reveal/open/share/drag workflows use canonical 9to1 file semantics. Interrupted downloads, retries and completion state remain visible and recoverable.
Split panes and tabs SHOULD support semantic drag/drop. Where both surfaces understand a canonical 9to1 entity, transfer the typed entity/link instead of degrading it to copied text. Examples include dragging a Maps place into Planner or a Board item into Write. Web upload targets may receive files through normal browser security/permission rules.
Sites can open project previews in Browse and Browse development context can offer Open project in Sites/Open source in Dev when the page is linked to a local project. Dev can launch localhost/development targets directly into Browse. Mature Firefox developer tools MUST be retained/adapted rather than replaced by a feature-poor custom inspector.
Security and origin isolation
cui://, browse:// and 9to1:// are privileged/non-web namespaces with separate routing and origin/capability rules. Ordinary HTTP(S) pages MUST NOT be able to inspect native app state, call privileged CUI/Browse APIs, forge trusted 9to1:// content or inherit internal permissions simply by navigating to or linking an internal route.
A web page may request navigation to an allowed registered internal route only through the normal navigation/policy boundary. Navigating to 9to1:// does not grant the originating site the destination app's authority. Profile cookies/credentials and engine-private state MUST remain isolated according to their owning profile/backend.
Recovery and degraded states
Browse MUST handle Firefox renderer crashes, Chromium renderer crashes, whole-browser crashes, failed engine startup, unavailable selected engines, extension incompatibility, interrupted downloads, invalid/corrupt engine-private state and failed engine switches without corrupting the other engine or canonical Browse profile state.
Session recovery SHOULD restore tabs, groups, workspaces, split arrangements, ProfileID and per-tab engine preference wherever safe. If a preferred engine is unavailable, Browse MUST surface the degraded state and offer a safe fallback rather than silently losing the tab or rewriting profile data.
Browse acceptance requirements
* Firefox donor parity remains present except for explicit 9to1 replacements/exclusions; proprietary Firefox AI surfaces are replaced by Dulche.
* Gecko-default and Chromium alternative rendering work within one canonical Browse tab/session model, with engine/profile isolation and per-site engine rules.
* Both upstream engine frameworks can update automatically through validated build/test/promotion and rollback pipelines.
* cui://, browse://, 9to1:// and HTTP(S) routes resolve to the correct security/content surface, including real native 9to1 app rendering inside tabs.
* Profiles can be mixed per tab, per workspace and inside Split View without cross-profile cookie/session leakage.
* Tab groups, split tabs and top/bottom/left/right tab-strip placement retain equivalent core functionality.
* browse://newtab provides the customisable widget/generative canvas, Search/AI switch and dual-provider split search.
* Dulche @ mentions resolve to canonical browser/app entities and permissioned autonomous browsing uses semantic browser capabilities with consequential-action safeguards.
* Extension compatibility states, extension CUI surfaces and Site Enhancer permissions behave explicitly and recoverably.
* Crash/session recovery preserves canonical Browse state and a failure in one renderer does not corrupt the other renderer/profile state.

source_text:
Mini Computer
Product role and shared virtualisation engine
9-1 Mini Computer is the native CUI virtual-computer and virtual-machine management app and the shared virtualisation engine used by Dev, Terminal and other authorised 9to1 surfaces. It supports creation, installation, import, execution, inspection, configuration, snapshots, cloning, networking, device integration, templates, developer workflows and recovery of supported virtual machines.
Mini Computer owns the canonical VirtualMachine/VirtualisationProvider model and VM lifecycle. Dev owns code/build/debug authoring, Terminal owns terminal sessions, Files owns user-addressable files/media identity and Home owns protected-action permission brokering.
A VM remains a real provider-backed virtual machine. Mini Computer MUST NOT replace mature hypervisor functionality with a simplified simulation merely to obtain a uniform UI.
Built-in default provider: 9to1 VirtualBox fork
The built-in and default provider is a maintained 9to1 fork of the VirtualBox Platform Package source. Mini Computer MUST include this provider so a user can create and run supported VMs without first installing or connecting a third-party hypervisor.
The implementation MUST fork and maintain the latest appropriate VirtualBox source in accordance with the global donor/upstream contract and the applicable open-source licence/third-party licence obligations. The fork remains an auditable upstream-derived backend rather than an opaque binary dependency with no source provenance.
VirtualBox's mature virtual-machine creation, configuration, storage, networking, snapshot, cloning, import/export, console and management behaviours are mandatory donor-parity inputs where supported by the target architecture/platform.
VirtualBox licensing and excluded separately licensed components
The 9to1 fork covers only VirtualBox source/components that CAKE is legally permitted to modify and distribute under their applicable licences. Separately licensed proprietary components such as the Oracle Extension Pack MUST NOT be copied, bundled or represented as part of the fork unless CAKE has obtained the required rights.
If a useful donor capability exists only in a separately licensed component, Mini Computer must either provide a legally independent 9to1-native replacement, support a separately user-installed/connected compatible component where lawful, or expose the capability as unavailable with a documented licensing/platform reason.
The implementation architecture SHOULD keep the fork/provider boundary sufficiently clear for licence compliance, update/rebase management and optional alternative-provider support.
Provider abstraction and optional connected providers
Mini Computer exposes a canonical VirtualisationProvider interface. The built-in 9to1 VirtualBox fork is selected by default, while users may connect/install additional compatible providers such as QEMU, KVM, Windows hypervisor integrations or extension-contributed providers when supported.
Provider has stable ProviderID, type/vendor, version, connection/install state, supported hosts/guest architectures, acceleration capabilities, firmware/security capabilities, device/network/storage features, import/export formats, debug/serial support and Revision.
Connecting another provider does not change the canonical VM semantics automatically. Each VM records ProviderID, and provider migration/conversion is an explicit operation with a preview of unsupported/lossy features.
Provider-specific advanced controls remain accessible through typed provider configuration without leaking arbitrary implementation flags into the canonical cross-provider model.
Provider capability matrix
Every provider reports exact capability state rather than relying on feature hiding alone. Capabilities include supported guest architectures, hardware acceleration, nested virtualisation, snapshots, live snapshots, saved state, cloning, disk formats/controllers, BIOS/UEFI, Secure Boot, TPM, USB/device passthrough, shared folders, clipboard/drag-drop, virtual networking, graphics acceleration, multi-monitor, audio, serial/debug interfaces and live configuration changes.
A setting unsupported by the active provider/platform is marked Unsupported/Unavailable with a reason and remediation/alternative where applicable. Mini Computer MUST NOT accept a setting and silently ignore it.
Capabilities may depend on host architecture and current host configuration, so provider/version support and effective host support are distinct states.
Canonical VirtualMachine model
VirtualMachine has stable VMID, name, ProviderID, EnvironmentID, guest OS metadata, architecture, machine/chipset type, firmware/security configuration, CPU configuration, memory configuration, storage controllers/disks/media, network adapters, display/GPU, audio, USB/devices, integration policy, shared folders, clipboard/drag-drop policy, snapshot graph, template/source provenance, lifecycle state, Files/resource references and Revision.
Renaming, moving in UI or changing provider display labels MUST NOT alter VMID. Provider-internal identifiers are retained as mappings rather than becoming the only canonical identity.
VM configuration is versioned and migratable. Unsupported/unknown future configuration is preserved/rejected explicitly rather than silently dropped.
VM lifecycle states
Canonical lifecycle states include at least PoweredOff, Starting, Running, Pausing, Paused, SavingState, Saved, Resuming, ShuttingDown, Stopping, Crashed, Disconnected/ViewerUnavailable and ProviderUnavailable where distinct.
Viewer state and VM state are separate. Closing or losing a viewer MUST NOT cause the UI to report PoweredOff if the VM remains running.
Lifecycle transitions are driven by verified provider state. Mini Computer MUST NOT report Start/Shutdown/Save successful until the provider confirms the resulting state or the operation explicitly remains Pending.

source_text:
Interactive VM viewer
Running VMs can open in an interactive Mini Computer viewer supporting keyboard, pointer capture/release, scaling, fullscreen, aspect handling, dynamic resolution when guest integration supports it and multi-monitor when the provider supports it.
The viewer may be embedded or popped out to a dedicated window while retaining the same VMID/session state.
Viewer disconnect/reconnect is separate from VM lifecycle and must not power off or duplicate the VM unless explicitly requested.
Power and state controls
Mini Computer distinguishes Start, Pause, Resume, Save State, ACPI/Guest Shutdown, Restart/Reset where supported and Power Off/Force Stop. The UI/API MUST NOT label destructive power-off as graceful shutdown.
Potential data-loss actions such as Power Off while a guest is running receive risk-appropriate confirmation unless a valid trust/policy explicitly covers them.
Power actions are idempotent or return AlreadyInState/InvalidState semantics rather than creating contradictory provider operations.
Snapshots
Snapshots are first-class canonical objects with stable SnapshotID, VMID, parent SnapshotID, name, description, creation time, provider reference, disk/memory-state coverage, guest state, size/retention metadata and Revision.
Users can create, inspect, restore, rename/descriptively edit where supported and delete/consolidate snapshots. Snapshot hierarchy is shown as a tree/graph rather than a flat list.
Restore explicitly states which disk/memory/config state is affected and what current unsaved state will be lost. External/shared resources not captured by the snapshot are clearly excluded.
Deleting/consolidating a snapshot MUST NOT silently delete a dependent branch/linked clone.
Cloning and linked clones
Mini Computer supports full clone and provider-supported linked clone from current state or a selected snapshot. Clone receives a new stable VMID and clear provenance.
Linked-clone dependency on base disks/snapshots is visible. Deleting/moving a required base is blocked or performs a deliberate consolidation/migration first.
Clone options include identity/network regeneration where needed to avoid duplicate machine identifiers.

source_text:
Display and graphics
Display configuration can expose virtual display controller, VRAM, monitor count, scaling, 2D/3D acceleration and provider-supported graphics features.
Ordinary virtual graphics acceleration is distinct from physical GPU passthrough. The latter uses its own provider/security/capability requirements.
Unsupported graphics settings remain visibly unavailable rather than being written into configuration and ignored.
Audio and microphone
Mini Computer exposes guest audio output/input routing where supported. Microphone input follows host privacy/device permission rules and MUST NOT silently activate because the VM starts.
Per-VM audio policy can disable input/output entirely for untrusted/test guests.
Clipboard and drag/drop trust policy
Shared clipboard and drag/drop support provider/guest-integration capabilities and explicit policies such as Disabled, HostToGuest, GuestToHost and Bidirectional.
These capabilities are disabled or conservatively configured by default according to security policy for untrusted guests. Guest integration installation alone MUST NOT silently enable bidirectional host data access.
Clipboard/drag-drop state is visible while the VM is running.
Shared folders
Users can expose host/Files-backed folders to guests through stable SharedFolder configurations with host/File identity, guest name/mount path, read-only/read-write, auto-mount and persistence policy.
Writable host sharing is a security boundary because guest software can modify host/user data. The UI/AI verification must make writable scope clear.
Deleting/moving a shared host resource resolves through Files identity where possible or leaves an explicit BrokenBinding state.
Guest integrations
Mini Computer detects and, where lawfully distributable/supported, can install appropriate guest integration tooling for dynamic resolution, clipboard, drag/drop, shared folders, guest status/shutdown and file transfer.
Guest integration version/health is visible. The VM remains operable when integrations are unavailable.
Mini Computer MUST NOT bundle separately licensed donor guest components without the necessary rights.

source_text:
Files and storage architecture
User-addressable Mini Computer resources are organised in Files through stable identities, conceptually including Machines, Disks, ISOs/Media, Templates and Exports. Exact physical layout may vary by storage provider but remains user-inspectable where appropriate.
Very large mutable virtual disks/snapshot chains may use a block/storage provider optimised for VM workloads rather than ordinary sync semantics. Provider-internal block state is not misrepresented as a normal small Files document.
Canonical VM/resource metadata records the mapping between user-visible Files resources and provider-internal storage so recovery/migration can distinguish source/configuration from derived/provider state.
Resource references and deduplication
Immutable installation media can be shared by reference across VMs. Linked/base virtual disks preserve explicit dependency identity rather than being duplicated or lost through path renames.
Moving/renaming a Files-backed ISO/export/template through supported Files/Mini Computer actions preserves references by stable ID.
Provider caches, temporary differencing layers and ephemeral development disks are marked derived/ephemeral and can be cleaned without deleting canonical user resources unless explicitly selected.
Terminal integration
Every supported VM can expose Open in Terminal for guest shell/SSH where configured, serial console, debug console or provider-supported command channel. This uses the shared Terminal engine.
Terminal creates/attaches an EnvironmentID tied to VMID/provider/guest channel and visibly identifies the VM so commands cannot be mistaken for host commands.
Closing Terminal does not power off the VM; VM lifecycle remains owned by Mini Computer.
Dev integration and Run target
Dev uses Mini Computer as the canonical VM runtime for projects whose RunConfiguration targets a VM. Dev MUST NOT maintain a parallel private hypervisor implementation.
For OS/kernel projects, Run can execute Build → package boot artifact → obtain/start configured Mini Computer VM → attach disk/ISO/EFI/kernel artifact → boot → expose viewer/serial/debug state.
Run configuration references stable VM/template/provider identities and can declare reset/snapshot/discard policy for repeatable development.
Ephemeral development VMs
Dev/CI can request ephemeral VMs derived from templates/snapshots for isolated testing. Policy can specify discard after success, preserve on failure, always preserve or snapshot-before-run.
Ephemeral instances receive unique VMID/runtime identity even when created from the same template and do not mutate the reusable template/base unintentionally.
Cleanup waits until logs/artifacts/checks referencing the ephemeral environment are retained or explicitly discarded.

source_text:
Accessibility
VM list, create wizard, settings, snapshots, networks, ISO Browser, provider status and power controls are keyboard-operable with screen-reader semantics.
VM lifecycle/provider/security state MUST NOT rely solely on colour or icons. Dangerous Power Off/Delete/Restore/Raw device actions have explicit accessible labels and consequences.
The embedded viewer provides accessible host controls around the guest even when guest OS accessibility itself is outside Mini Computer's control.
Performance and scalability
VM lists, snapshots, ISO/media libraries and monitoring views are virtualised/paged where needed. UI rendering MUST NOT require loading every virtual disk/snapshot into memory.
Provider operations such as import/export, clone, disk conversion, large download, snapshot consolidation and migration run as cancellable/resumable jobs where the provider supports it, with stable JobID/progress/error state.
Mini Computer remains responsive while one or more VMs generate heavy I/O or console output.
Recovery and failure behaviour
Mini Computer distinguishes viewer disconnect, provider service failure, VM crash, host-resource exhaustion, disk/media missing, storage corruption and configuration incompatibility rather than collapsing them into VM failed.
Reopening after UI crash/restart re-discovers provider-managed running/saved VMs by stable mapping and reattaches without duplication where the provider can prove identity.
Structured failures include VMNotFound, ProviderUnavailable, ProviderCapabilityUnavailable, HardwareVirtualisationUnavailable, AccelerationUnavailable, InvalidVMState, DiskNotFound, DiskDependencyBlocked, MediaNotFound, MediaIntegrityFailed, MediaAcquisitionNotPermitted, SnapshotDependencyBlocked, SnapshotRestoreConflict, NetworkConflict, DeviceUnavailable, HostResourceRisk, CredentialUnavailable, ImportUnsupported, ExportFailed, ViewerDisconnected, GuestIntegrationUnavailable, RevisionConflict, PermissionDenied and CapabilityUnavailable plus provider-specific diagnostic codes.
Partial provider/storage operations return succeeded/failed/remaining resources and recovery steps; Mini Computer MUST NOT report rollback/cleanup success unless verified.
Platform capability behaviour
Windows, 9to1-OS and other supported desktop hosts preserve the same canonical VM/provider/media model while capability-negotiating the built-in VirtualBox fork, hardware acceleration, host networking, device passthrough and filesystem/storage behaviour.
Web surfaces may manage/view remote Mini Computer providers/VMs when an authorised remote execution provider exists but MUST NOT pretend the browser itself can provide unrestricted local hardware virtualisation.
Unsupported architecture/provider combinations are explicit release/platform exceptions rather than silent missing UI.
When Home is absent at process start, Mini Computer follows the global Install Home/bootstrap contract.

Write is implementation-complete only when its exhaustive applicable stage/platform manifest and APP-AC gates pass. The following WRITE-AC requirements and existing criteria are mandatory minimum coverage, not a replacement for complete donor parity and the full specified Write product.
WRITE-AC-001 — Non-substitutable word processor. For Part 1 RCVP, launch the real CUI Write app from normal entry points with the integrated LibreOffice Writer/LibreOfficeKit donor engine and canonical storage. A plain multiline input, Markdown/contenteditable editor, list of separately styled Text controls, command panel, test host or external donor window is not Write. Formatting must change the selected document runs/paragraphs/objects and render through the real document model; modifying only toolbar state or metadata is failure. Preserve donor-capable editing, selections, rich clipboard, IME, undo/redo, layout, accessible navigation, persistence and supported interchange. All applicable donor baseline features must remain discoverable and usable through the intended CUI product, not only backend APIs.
WRITE-AC-002 — Authentic integrated workflow and artifact inspection. In the shipped editor, create/open a realistic multi-paragraph document; move the caret and select independent ranges; apply different inline formatting and paragraph/custom styles; edit a real multi-cell table; insert and manipulate an image with anchoring/wrapping; exercise undo/redo, keyboard navigation, find/replace and representative review/reference features. Save, close the app, restart and reopen; compare semantic structure and rendered results. Import and export representative DOCX and ODT using the actual engines, reopen exports in an independent compatible reader, and inspect PDF export visually and structurally. A filename, success message, JSON surrogate or saved plain text is not proof of the promised file format. Inspect real output contents, styles, table structure, images and layout; record losses explicitly and block acceptance for unsupported mandatory fidelity. These journeys supplement the exhaustive donor manifest; they do not reduce it to the named examples.
WRITE-AC-003 — Specified shell, stage boundaries and Full acceptance. The real editor uses the stated title/backstage entry, stable floating contextual toolbar, persistent +/Eye/overflow controls, context-relevant actions, document work surface and shared AI bar; it is not a permanent ribbon or generic demonstration dashboard. Launch/start and editor MUST independently satisfy LAUNCH-001–006 and APP-AC-009, with separate runtime evidence and real navigation; a start-page heading above the document surface is a rejection case. Keep Sections/navigation, contextual menus, document views, layout controls and accessibility integrated as their stage requirements become available; non-implemented Full features remain openly tracked, never fictitious controls. Part 1 RCVP may defer only new 9to1 enhancements assigned to Part 2 by the active directive. Part 2 Full must independently verify all specified Sections, Continuous/Pages/Book, Locked/Unlocked, custom text/table styles, PDF editing, review/collaboration, AI, interoperability and remaining Write requirements. View/theme changes must preserve canonical content, identity and selection. UI controls, typed APIs and resulting artifacts must demonstrate the same real operations.

source_text:
Present
Purpose, ownership and conformance
9-1 Present is the CUI presentation authoring, presenting and interactive-runtime application. LibreOffice Impress/Draw is the donor foundation for applicable mature presentation editing, interoperability and quality-of-life behaviour. 9-1 owns the CUI shell, the native .9to1p model, the Actions runtime, typed APIs, AI integration, component model and cross-app semantics.
Applicable donor functionality MUST be preserved unless a scoped donor-parity exception is recorded in the canonical donor-parity manifest. Present MUST NOT ship as a reduced slide editor whose only conformance evidence is file opening or basic text/shape editing.
Present MUST use Home's Shared Productivity Engine for every registered shared object type that it supports. Shared text, tables, charts/graphs, images/media, drawings/ink and other shared objects copied between Present, Write, Canvas, Boards and Spaces MUST preserve the shared object schema, semantic identifiers, formatting, accessibility metadata and clipboard representation.
Release boundary:
* Present owns PresentationID, SlideID, slide order, slide composition, presentation-level state, slide-local state, speaker notes references, presentation sessions and the Actions graph.
* Home owns shared productivity object schemas, permission brokerage, shared AI/runtime services, common clipboard bundles and other platform services defined in Home.
* Present MUST NOT introduce a second private implementation of a Home-owned shared object or platform service.
* The native .9to1p representation is authoritative for full-fidelity 9-1 behaviour.
Normative applicability and capability negotiation
Terms such as applicable, supported and available are not discretionary escape hatches in this section. They are resolved from explicit manifests or runtime capability declarations.
* A donor feature is applicable unless it is classified in the Present donor-parity manifest as Replace with 9-1-native equivalent or Not applicable with a recorded technical/legal reason.
* A platform capability is supported only when the platform capability registry declares the required capability and version for the active device/runtime.
* A file-format construct is representable only when the import/export capability matrix declares a mapping for the source construct and target format/version.
* Failure of a required capability check MUST produce a typed unavailable/unsupported result and the specified fallback or CompatibilityIssue; silent omission is prohibited.
* An implementation MUST NOT reinterpret a MUST requirement as optional merely because its current code path does not implement the required capability.
Landing page, file lifecycle and persistence
Present MUST implement the global launch-screen contract. The launch surface MUST expose Create New, Open/Import, recent presentations and real template/theme discovery. Recent items MUST be derived from persisted history; fabricated recent files are prohibited except for explicitly labelled onboarding or template content.
The release file contract MUST support native .9to1p plus PPTX and ODP import/export. Static output MUST support PDF and image export. Present MUST provide complete create -> edit -> save -> close -> reopen workflows with autosave, crash/interrupted-save recovery, revision tracking and conflict-safe persistence.
* A failed save, partial media write, unresolved revision conflict or recovery failure MUST be surfaced as an explicit error state.
* Present MUST NOT report success until the target revision and all referenced persisted objects required for the save have been committed.
* Recovery MUST preserve the last known-good durable revision and MUST NOT overwrite it with a partially reconstructed presentation.

source_text:
Data
Product role and data paradigms
9-1 Data is the native CUI spreadsheet, structured-data, relational-database, SQL-query and analytical workspace. It combines conventional spreadsheet work, rich structured cells, relational modelling, multidimensional analytical data, charts/pivots, data transformation, database exploration and AI-assisted analysis in one coherent product.
Data MUST support four native data paradigms without forcing one paradigm onto every project: spreadsheet/grid data, relational database data, hierarchical/rich structured data and multidimensional analytical data. These paradigms may interoperate through explicit projections, relationships and transformations, but their semantics MUST NOT be silently conflated.
The ordinary spreadsheet remains the approachable default. Advanced relational, nested, multidimensional and query capabilities appear when the data or user workflow requires them. Native .9to1d projects MAY represent richer structures than XLSX/ODS; compatibility formats MUST NOT constrain the native model.
Shared engines, donor source and implementation authority
LibreOffice Calc is the spreadsheet-compatibility/donor engine for established spreadsheet behaviour, formula compatibility and XLSX/ODS interoperability. DuckDB is the local analytical SQL engine for local tables, files, queries and relational projections. Configured providers MAY add PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite, SQL Server and other supported external database systems through typed connection adapters.
The 9to1 source tree MUST contain or fetch the appropriate maintained LibreOffice Calc donor source required by the architecture, subject to the global donor-source and licensing contract. The implementation agent MUST NOT treat a missing LibreOffice installation or missing checked-out donor source as permission to build a miniature replacement spreadsheet engine. If the required donor source is absent during an autonomous development pass, the agent MUST obtain/fork the latest appropriate compatible source and record the exact upstream/version used before continuing dependent implementation.
Data MUST integrate donor capability into the 9to1 product model, CUI and typed APIs. Merely shelling out to soffice as an opaque external black box while leaving the canonical Data experience or API surface incomplete does not satisfy the implementation requirement.
Shared charting, Node Graph, Files, identity/permissions, credential storage, AI/model, action/audit and other cross-product infrastructure MUST be reused where canonical rather than privately reimplemented.
Canonical Data project model
DataProject has stable ProjectID, Workbooks[], DataSources[], Connections[], SavedQueries[], DataModels[], TransformPipelines[], DataCubes[], Visualisations[], Charts[], PivotModels[], project settings, CreatedAt, ModifiedAt and Revision.
A project MAY contain only a workbook, only database/query resources, only a multidimensional model, or any compatible combination. A user MUST NOT need to create unrelated projects merely because one analysis starts in a spreadsheet and later uses SQL or a transformation pipeline.
Data resources reference stable identities rather than UI coordinates wherever the resource has independent semantic identity. Ordinary A1/R1C1-style references remain available for spreadsheet compatibility, but tables, records, queries, charts, pivots, connections, relationships, visualisations and pipelines have stable IDs.
Workbook and spreadsheet model
Workbook has stable WorkbookID, Sheets[], workbook names/named ranges, calculation settings, external/link metadata, compatibility metadata and Revision.
Sheet has stable SheetID, ordered rows/columns/cells, tables, drawings/charts where applicable, filters, freeze state, view state and Revision. Reordering or renaming a sheet MUST NOT invalidate stable references that use SheetID.
Cells support ordinary scalar values, formulas, formatting, validation, comments/notes, hyperlinks/references and compatible Calc spreadsheet features. Grid coordinates identify a location in a sheet; they are not the sole identity mechanism for richer Data objects.
Normal spreadsheet workflows include direct cell/formula-bar editing, fill/copy, pattern autofill, insert/delete rows and columns, row/column resize/hide/freeze, multi-range selection, find/replace, sort/filter, named ranges, tables, validation/dropdowns, conditional formatting, comments/notes, sheet management, protection where compatible and undo/redo.

source_text:
Data sources and connections
Data distinguishes static/imported data, linked files, project-local queryable data and external/live connections. Static/imported sources include declared CSV/TSV/JSON where supported and spreadsheet formats. Local query sources include DuckDB-accessible tables/files such as CSV/Parquet where supported. External/live connections use typed provider adapters.
DataSource and Connection objects have stable identity, provider/dialect, scope, capability metadata, source schema/version information where available and refresh state. Credentials/secrets MUST use the 9to1 credential/trust infrastructure and MUST NOT be embedded in .9to1d project content, query history or ordinary logs.
Connection capability negotiation defines supported transactions, snapshots/checkpoints, schema introspection, DDL/DML features, explain plans, cancellation and backup/recovery options.
SQL workspace
Data MUST provide native SQL authoring/execution with syntax highlighting, dialect-aware parsing/validation, schema/object browser, table/column/function completion, relationship-aware join suggestions, query formatting, parameters where supported, saved queries, query history, execution timing/statistics, cancellation, paged/virtualised result sets, EXPLAIN/plan access where supported and result export/materialisation.
DuckDB SHOULD make local analytical querying nearly frictionless: eligible project tables and supported local files can be queried directly without requiring users to provision an external database.
SQL results can be inspected, opened in Visualise, saved as a query, materialised to a sheet/table, exported or used as downstream transformation input.
Persistent AI / SQL bar switcher
In Data, the persistent floating input bar contains an explicit mode switcher between AI and SQL. AI mode routes natural-language requests through Dulche and typed Data actions. SQL mode treats the input as SQL and executes it natively against the explicitly selected SQL target; SQL text MUST NOT be sent to AI merely to emulate execution.
SQL mode MUST always display the active execution target, for example DuckDB · This Project or PostgreSQL · Production. The selected connection/database/schema scope MUST be visible enough that users cannot reasonably confuse a local analytical target with a live external target.
Changing the SQL execution target is explicit. Data MUST NOT silently retarget a query because another sheet, panel or connection became focused.
Native SQL execution records and results
Every execution creates a canonical SqlExecution record with stable ExecutionID, ConnectionID/target, dialect, statements, classification, ReadOnly state, initiator, start/completion state, result sets, affected objects/rows where known, recovery strategy/reference where applicable, transaction/savepoint metadata, outcome/error and audit reference.
SQL result sets preserve typed columns and support virtualised/paged browsing. Successful prior result state MUST remain available when a later execution fails unless the user explicitly replaces/discards it.
Query history records target, dialect, classification, result metadata and outcome without storing secrets. SavedQuery objects are persistent editable query resources with stable identity.
Read-only and mutating SQL classification
Data MUST parse/classify SQL before execution. Provably read-only statements such as ordinary SELECT/CTE SELECT, EXPLAIN and supported metadata introspection MAY execute directly subject to connection permissions.
Potentially mutating or schema-changing SQL includes INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE and provider-specific mutation commands. Classification MUST be conservative when the dialect/parser cannot prove a statement is read-only.
Multi-statement input is treated as one explicit execution plan with per-statement classification and declared atomicity/partial-execution risk.
Protected live-database SQL execution
Consequential SQL against an external/live database enters the protected execution path. Before execution Data MUST identify the target, classify statements, inspect likely affected objects, use a transaction/savepoint where supported, determine preview/impact information where technically possible, establish an appropriate recoverable backup/checkpoint strategy when required, show the effect/recovery state and obtain the applicable confirmation.
Recovery strategy is backend-aware and may use transaction rollback, savepoint, affected-row before-image capture, table snapshot/copy, database-native snapshot, backup file/provider recovery point, schema export plus affected data or another verified recoverable mechanism. Data MUST record the strategy actually established.
If the safety contract for the requested live mutation requires rollback/backup protection and Data cannot establish it, execution MUST stop. Data MUST NOT state or imply that a backup, transaction or rollback exists when it does not.
After execution Data verifies the actual outcome where feasible, records audit/recovery information and truthfully reports partial success/failure. It MUST NOT blindly retry consequential SQL without operation identity/idempotency or renewed confirmation where required.
DDL and dependency impact
Schema-changing SQL receives dependency-aware analysis where metadata is available. Before consequential DROP/ALTER/rename operations Data SHOULD identify dependent views, foreign keys, indexes, saved queries, linked Data views, Forms integrations, Visualisations and other known references.
DDL impact that cannot be determined reliably MUST be represented as unknown rather than assumed safe.
Manual SQL versus AI-proposed SQL
Direct SQL typed and executed by the user remains native SQL interaction and is not treated as an AI mutation merely because it is entered in the shared bar. Read-only SQL should not acquire unnecessary AI-style approval friction.
AI may draft, explain, optimise, fix or generate SQL, but an AI-proposed consequential mutation MUST NOT bypass Data's per-action approval rules. For external database changes, the proposed SQL and target/impact/recovery information MUST be inspectable before approved execution.
If AI decides SQL is the best implementation of a Data task, the generated SQL remains visible/inspectable and execution occurs through the same SQL safety pipeline rather than an opaque hidden database mutation.

source_text:
Recovery and failure behaviour
Project/workbook saves and schema changes MUST be crash-safe. Failed imports, refreshes, transforms, SQL executions, exports or Visualise calculations MUST leave previous valid canonical data intact unless the user explicitly accepted a destructive operation whose partial effects are truthfully reported.
Structured failures include ProjectNotFound, WorkbookNotFound, SheetNotFound, TableNotFound, RecordNotFound, InvalidFormula, CircularReference, SchemaViolation, ConstraintViolation, RelationshipViolation, ConnectionUnavailable, AuthenticationRequired, SqlParseError, SqlExecutionFailed, MutationProtectionUnavailable, BackupFailed, RollbackFailed, PartialCommit, RefreshFailed, TransformFailed, VisualisationIncompatible, ExportCompatibilityLoss, RevisionConflict, PermissionDenied and CapabilityUnavailable plus provider/backend errors.
Data MUST distinguish 'rollback attempted' from 'rollback succeeded'. Recovery/audit metadata remains inspectable after failure.
Platform capability behaviour
Windows, 9to1-OS and web preserve the same canonical Data project/workbook/schema/query/pipeline/cube/Visualisation model while capability-negotiating local DuckDB execution, LibreOffice-derived compatibility components, external database drivers, file access and hardware/resource differences.
A platform that cannot execute a particular local/provider capability MUST expose CapabilityUnavailable or route to an explicitly configured supported service; it MUST NOT silently substitute incompatible semantics.
When Home is absent at process start, Data follows the global Install Home/bootstrap contract rather than launching an incompatible private runtime.

source_text:
Canonical geospatial entities
Maps MUST define stable canonical entities rather than allowing each app to store copied address strings. At minimum, the typed model must cover Place, Address, Coordinate, Route, RouteLeg, RouteStep, SavedPlace, PersonalLandmark, CommunityPOI, MapView, SearchResult, SearchProvider, MapProviderReference and SavedRoute/CustomJourney or equivalent strongly typed contracts.
A Place may reference one or more provider records, OpenStreetMap objects, community objects or user-authored data without making any single provider identifier the canonical 9to1 identity. Provider records are provenance references, not the primary identity of a saved 9to1 entity.
Planner, Events, Spaces, Boards, Write, Present, Forms, Automations and other apps MUST reference canonical Place/Route/Landmark IDs through typed APIs where a persistent location relationship is required.
Search / AI interaction
Maps MUST use the same explicit Search / AI interaction pattern established elsewhere in 9to1. Search is the default mode. The selected mode is always visible and can be switched immediately without losing the selected place, route or current map context.
Search mode performs deterministic geographic discovery and manual route construction. It must search, as applicable, addresses, postcodes, coordinates, named places, businesses/POIs, categories, saved places, PersonalLandmarks, CommunityPOIs and supported 9to1 entities with attached locations. Provider result confidence and ambiguity MUST remain visible; Maps MUST NOT fabricate an exact address or place identity from weak geocoding.
Selecting a result opens a canonical place/details surface with provenance and relevant actions such as View, Navigate, Add to route, Set as start, Set as destination, Add stop, Save, Share and other capability-appropriate actions.
AI mode is a Dulche-backed natural-language Maps interface operating the same canonical Maps state and APIs. Requests such as 'take me to the nearest Starbucks', 'find somewhere quiet to study within a 15-minute walk', 'find a bench along this route' or 'add a coffee stop halfway home' MUST be resolved through real search/location/routing capabilities rather than invented model knowledge.
A request such as 'take me to the nearest Starbucks' should resolve the permitted current location, search real place providers, rank valid candidates according to the user's request and actual route/travel distance where available, resolve the chosen candidate to a canonical Place, calculate a route and start/present navigation according to the explicit user intent. If multiple interpretations materially affect the result, Maps must present candidates or request the minimum necessary disambiguation rather than guessing.
Search and AI are interoperable. A place found manually can become AI context, and an AI-generated route/place remains a normal canonical Maps object that the user can inspect, edit, reorder, save or share manually.
Saved places and personal landmarks
Users can save ordinary provider/OpenStreetMap places and create PersonalLandmarks anywhere on the map. A PersonalLandmark does not require an existing mapped place, recognised address, road, POI or provider object; a coordinate and user-defined identity are sufficient.
Users MUST be able to drop a pin at any coordinate, name it, optionally categorise it, add notes/metadata, save it privately, share it explicitly and navigate to it. Examples include a meeting point, favourite viewpoint, shortcut entrance, personal picnic spot or a specific bench.
Common saved places such as Home, College, Church or Work are canonical SavedPlace references. Other apps resolve these references through Maps rather than retaining independent copies of the underlying address.
Personal/private landmarks are private by default. Creating a private landmark MUST NOT implicitly publish its coordinates, name, notes or category to the community database or an external provider.
